item.title: Elisa Nuyten’s Vega Foundation Is Quietly Reshaping the World of Moving-Image Art - ARTnews.com
item.description:
To describe the plight of artists who make films and videos, Martine Syms compared the situation to a viral meme starring a giant, vacant head waiting to be filled in with words below a familiar prompt: “Why you so quiet? What’s on your mind?” For her part, Syms said she would fill in that empty noggin with some stark words: “I’m trying to fund my no-budget experimental film.”

There has never been an especially easy time to make moving-image art, which is notoriously hard to monetize. But these days, the challenge is even more formidable because of the abundance of film and video art in the context of biennials, museums, and the art discourse more broadly.

Syms should know. For more than a decade, she has conceived acclaimed videos, installations, and performances about identity, often with a focus on Blackness and meme culture. Such work has earned her representation by three blue-chip galleries, and her 2022 feature film The African Desperate was theatrically distributed by Mubi, the company that would spin the Demi Moore–starring horror movie The Substance into a surprise Oscar contender two years later. She will also be the subject of a Museum of Contemporary Art Los Angeles survey next year.

But Syms said she still faces a widespread lack of understanding about film/video work and the shortage of funding to accompany it. “I had a collector in Europe ask, ‘Why should I buy video art?’” she told me. “I was like, ‘I don’t fucking know.’” (She later clarified that she hadn’t felt compelled to dignify that collector with an answer, saying, “It has nothing to do with me.”)

The problem is not unique to her, either. When ARTnews surveyed the best artworks of the 21st century so far in 2025, six of the top 10 pieces were moving-image works. One of those was Grosse Fatigue (2013), a widely shown video essay by Camille Henrot about the creation of the universe represented through images and videos clicked open on a computer desktop. Henrot, who debuted her first follow-up moving-image work after more than a decade earlier this year, said that support for such work remains hard to come by, even after endorsements from international institutions and representation by the mega-gallery Hauser & Wirth. She recently told Art in America, ARTnews’s sister publication, “I saw someone commenting about the current art market crisis, suggesting that what sells now is experiences, and also works that are easy to transport. I was like, wait! I have your medium! Film!”

When Syms and I spoke in the spring, I asked why acclaimed video artists like she and Henrot face such trouble. “The big answer, I guess, is that it’s a market imperative,” she said. “Increasingly, there are investors that galleries are reporting to—stakeholder interests. It’s a bigger thing that’s happening across moving images.” She added, “There’s really no way to fund low-budget work.”

Here to help improve the situation, at least in part, is the Vega Foundation, a Toronto-based art organization founded by collector Elisa Nuyten. Vega has supported video artists such as Syms by commissioning new works and showing them in institutions and biennials before adding them to its own collection. For Syms—and other notable artists including Lucy Raven, Jordan Strafer, and Stephanie Comilang—the Vega Foundation has become a lifeline.

Syms is currently at work on a new commission from Vega that will appear in her survey at MOCA LA: RW-LO, which she described as a “film about a Real World superfan in Y2K New Orleans.” (She described the work as being “inspired by a true story,” since the hit MTV reality show’s ninth season was shot in the Big Easy in the year 2000, and added, “I was myself a Real World superfan.”)

Syms said she spent nearly 20 years conceiving the work but it was only recently that the Vega Foundation helped make the project a reality. Having struck up a conversation with the foundation several years ago, she approached Vega with a version of a script. Without much delay, the foundation gave her funding. “They’ve been great to work with,” Syms said. “They’re the best kind of collaborator.”

“I do feel that video art is under-supported,” Nuyten, a new addition to the ARTnews Top 200 Collectors list, said in April, speaking from her home in Paris (she splits her time between there and Toronto). She was quick to note that she was surrounded by paintings and sculptures—a landscape by Miriam Cahn and an aquarium by Pierre Huyghe, for example. There were notably few videos, which she conceded can be “hard to live with.” She added: “Collectors often stay away from the medium. That’s why we quickly rose in the art world. Artists like talking to us.”

Founded in 2022, Vega is not the only organization of its kind—there’s also the Fondazione In Between Art Film and the LAS Foundation, both of which were launched in 2019 by collectors (Beatrice Bulgari for the former; Jan Fischer for the latter, working in association with Bettina Kames). But the Vega Foundation stands out as a leader in the field, with commissions regularly popping up in biennials and museums. Often, the only way to know about the foundation’s involvement in a project is to read the fine print on a wall text. Still, Vega’s behind-the-scenes efforts have helped to shape video art as it stands today.

One of the foundation’s first commissions was for Ali Cherri, a Lebanese artist whose Vega-supported film The Dam (2022) centers on a Sundanese bricklayer who, in his spare time, begins making a mud creation near the Nile. The film showed in the 2022 Venice Biennale, where it won the Silver Lion for an emerging artist; the jury praised Cherri’s work for its ability to bring “a meditation on earth, fire and water from a constructive perspective to a mythical dimension.” That same year, a version of it was screened at the Cannes Film Festival.

More recently, Vega helped fund Diego Marcon’s Krapfen (2025), a film in which a child is taunted by invisible beings that sing and dance. (Marcon, a young Italian artist with a flair for eerie, exquisite absurdism, rendered those beings as see-through by using green-screen technology.) Krapfen made its debut in 2025 at the Renaissance Society in Chicago, where Newcity praised it as a “must-see,” and then formed the centerpiece of a Marcon solo show that opened this past summer at the Art Gallery of Ontario and will soon travel to New York’s New Museum, where Nuyten is a trustee.

Between the Cherri and Marcon works, Vega commissioned artists such as Sharon Lockhart, an American filmmaker who used the foundation’s funding to shoot on Fogo Island, off the coast of Newfoundland; Alia Farid, a Kuwaiti biennial-circuit staple whose Vega project took her to southern Iraq; and Aria Dean, a rising American star whose widely praised video Abattoir, U.S.A.! (2023) centers on a slaughterhouse that she rendered digitally; and Lap-See Lam, a Swedish phenom whose films have pondered aspects of the Chinese diaspora. Vega’s adventurous support continued this year with a new commission by Yuyan Wang, who unveiled a film about robots and animatronics as part of a show organized by the Fondazione In Between Art Film in Venice.

Julia Paoli, the Vega Foundation’s curator, said she decides which projects to fund based in part on studio visits with artists. “We’re really trying to understand what artists are thinking through and working on, and also what our colleagues and peers are thinking about, so that we can stay rigorous,” she said. She also considers whether an artist or their work bears any connection to Canada, or whether a potential video commission could be presented with a partner institution there.

Otherwise, Paoli noted few parameters for a Vega commission, saying that each budget is tailor-made to its recipient. The budgets also come with a plan for where to present the work, be it a biennial, a film festival, or a museum. “We’re talking about the production of incredibly rigorous, complicated work, so I’m coming at it from a deeply researched curatorial perspective,” Paoli said of such expensive and time-consuming projects. “These are high-stakes.”

The Vega Foundation grew out of Nuyten’s collecting. Raised in Belgium, she started Vitamine Chic, a wholesale fashion agency in Toronto that she ran from 1988 until she sold it in 1998. Around 20 years ago, while traveling in Europe, Nuyten began buying art. “I decided I wanted to apply myself to contemporary art and learn about it,” she said. “I didn’t have an art history degree, but I went to local galleries. Slowly, I started to travel more and to collect more. I wanted art on my walls—I wanted interesting things for my children, and for us as a family, to respond to.”

Nuyten’s collection now includes quite a bit of historical art, by artists ranging from the Surrealist painter Leonor Fini to the French sculptor Louise Bourgeois, as well as works by some of today’s most famous living artists: Sarah Lucas, Philippe Parreno, Luc Tuymans, and others. But Nuyten spoke most highly of the “younger generations of artists” working today, many of whom are attracted to video. Starting the Vega Foundation was an attempt to connect with such stars in the making. “It was a very easy decision,” Nuyten said. “I felt that it would allow me to stay relevant” and reach “more experimental, more political voices.”

She was specific about the political aspect of what she does, recalling that amid Israel’s war in Gaza she told her colleagues at Vega Foundation, “Let’s support the film of a great Palestinian artist.” With Palestinian artists facing pushback, and in some cases censorship, in mainstream institutions, Vega threw its support behind the Berlin-based filmmaker Basma Al-Sharif, whose 2025 commission Morning Circle focuses on an Armenian man and his Jordanian son in Germany. Though the film doesn’t directly address the war in Gaza, it was politicized in Germany. When al-Sharif screened it at the Kunstakademie Düsseldorf this year, Jewish organizations and conservative politicians issued public denouncements of both the artist and the storied art school, in what the artist Adam Broomberg and writer Michele Faguet described as a “smear campaign” in a Hyperallergic defense of al-Sharif’s film. In mind of supporting work of the kind, Nuyten said, “We want to help. We can be more political with our organization.”

The Vega Foundation is currently gearing up for its fifth year, and Nuyten has been thinking about its future. “I don’t want to become the LUMA Foundation,” she said, referring to collector Maja Hoffmann’s long-running art organization that went on to open a Frank Gehry–designed museum in Arles, France. “I don’t want to open a space.”

Asked why not, she scrunched up her face. “To have a permanent space, that almost makes me feel a bit claustrophobic. It would be so non-dynamic—the opposite of what we want to be.”

A version of this article that appeared in print stated that Basma Al-Sharif’s film focused on Palestinian woman. In fact, it centers on an Armenian father and his Jordanian son.

item.title: New York Public Library Gets Over 250 Kiki Smith Prints, a Gift from the Artist’s Sister Seton Smith - ARTnews.com
item.description:
Thanks to the generosity of a sibling, the New York Public Library (NYPL) is now the owner of some 250 prints by Kiki Smith. They come as the gift of her sister, fellow artist Seton Smith, who has pledged to give all future prints she receives by Kiki to the institution.

The library’s Prints and Spencer Collections already have 30 other Smith prints and 12 of her artist’s books, and with the new gift, including works from as far back as the 1990s and into the present, the library will have one of the most concentrated holdings of the artist’s printed oeuvre in the United States.

“I am very thrilled by my sister Seton Smith’s gift to the New York Public Library because I could think of no more wonderful place for my prints to be,” said Kiki Smith in press materials. “Public libraries are to be cherished.”

The daughter of sculptor Tony Smith, Kiki Smith is a major art historical figure, represented by international gallery Pace, whose founder, Arne Glimcher, mounted a show of her work at his 125 Newbury Gallery in New York just this year. Jan Avgikos wrote in Artforum that in one part of the show, “Smith’s meditations on life and temporality were threaded with wonder at the ineffability of the natural world,” while describing another as “a magnificently gruesome memory theater—one that registered our failure to live together with our own transgressions.”

Smith has appeared in five Venice Biennales, and her work is included in museum collections internationally, from the Albertina in Vienna to the Art Institute of Chicago, the Pompidou in Paris, New York’s Museum of Modern Art, and the National Gallery of Art in Washington, D.C.

As Nancy Hass wrote in the New York Times in 2018, Smith “has, over the years, woven from glass, bronze, paper, glitter, steel, lead, clay and thread a vast, all-encompassing universe of enchantment, religious ecstasy and personal mythology.”

Smith got her start in the late 1980s and 1990s. Madeleine Viljoen, curator of the NYPL’s Prints and Spencer Collections, said in an email that “Informed by medical texts like Gray’s Anatomy, the works [Smith] produced during this period focused on the human body, featuring often graphic prints of individual organs, blood vessels, cellular forms, and bodily fluids. Rooted in feminism and unfolding against the backdrop of the AIDS crisis, the works consider flesh and the human body with brutal honesty, viewing them as vessels for trauma, mortality, and political autonomy. By the late 1990s, her work began to explore folklore, mythology and religion from a feminist perspective.”

The NYPL will treat the works quite differently from what one might expect at an art museum.

“We see these materials as art but also materials of study,” said Julie Golia, director of the humanities and social sciences research library, in a video conversation. “Anyone can come in with a library card and spend time with these materials, not behind glass but as a researcher. That kind of access is our special sauce here at 42nd Street.”

The NYPL is a partner in Art Week NYC, a citywide gathering celebrating New York’s leading galleries, institutions, and cultural spaces, organized by ARTnews, Art in America, and Artforum. The inaugural event takes place from November 11–14, 2026.

item.title: The Best Booths at Art Basel Paris, From Tar Paintings to a Falling Knife - ARTnews.com
item.description:
Across some 200 booths at Art Basel Paris this year, there is a lot to take in. As the Swiss company’s French fair matures, galleries have begun to bring more and more top-tier, high-priced works, which in turn has made it less a place to discover something new than a place for six-, seven-, and even eight-figure works to be sold. And during the Avant-Première VVIP preview on Tuesday afternoon, exhibiting galleries reported quite a few sales, which they would add to by the close of business Wednesday.

While the fair can be a bit market-darling-heavy on the ground floor, be sure to visit the upstairs, where some of the best works on view can be found. And if nothing strikes your fancy, you can at least look up and take in the beauty of the Grand Palais’s green-painted, steel-and-glass ceiling.

Below, a look at the best booths at Art Basel Paris, which runs through October 25 at the Grand Palais.

item.title: The French Student Protesters Subverting Monuments Like It's May 68 - Hyperallergic
item.description:
When students in France took to the streets in 1968 to protest the country's crumbling education system and Gaullist government, they transformed public statues into participants in their cause. After the May 2 shuttering of Paris Nanterre University, where anti-imperialist students began protests in late March that year, demonstrators took to the Sorbonne, where they hung portraits of Karl Marx, Vladimir Lenin, and Chairman Mao Zedong from the 17th-century facade’s pillars and lodged red revolutionary flags into the statues of scientist Louis Pasteur and writer Victor Hugo. During a May 13 demonstration coinciding with a national general strike, other protesters climbed atop Léopold Morice's "Monument à la République" (1883), which depicts Marianne, the personification of the French Republic, and staked out the artwork as a gathering ground for fellow protesters.

Today, student demonstrators in France are addressing many of the same issues at the heart of May 68, from underresourced schools to a worsening cost-of-living crisis — and are similarly incorporating public statues, monuments, and culturally significant sites into their actions. Earlier this month, protesters draped the "Monument à la République" in a white garment reading, "Neglected high schools, youth sacrificed," denouncing poor labor conditions, staff shortages, and grueling hours in the education system. 

On October 19, dozens of students from the École du Louvre, a higher education arts institution in the Louvre Palace in Paris, blocked the main entrance of the Louvre Museum. And in Marseille, a separate group knocked a bust of Marianne to the floor after breaking into Marseille City Hall.

Elsewhere, protesters have dressed statues in garments referencing other social movements, making broader, historical appeals to France’s long protest tradition. On October 17, organizers gave Marianne a wardrobe change, opting for a yellow vest bearing the message, "2026: The police mutilates high schoolers." A reference to the self-described gilets jaunes (“yellow vests”) who took to the streets in 2018–20 in protest of rising fuel prices and the unaddressed plights of ordinary citizens, the display underscored the longstanding and growing fissures between the public and police, who have overwhelmingly arrested minors and injured hundreds of students since protests began. French rights groups and lawyers have accused police of inflicting "war-like injuries" on teenagers: Riot officers maimed a 14-year-old boy with a tear gas grenade in a Parisian suburb and beat others with batons, among other violent methods. 

Demonstrators at the Place de la République streaked the eyes of the allegorical maidens Liberty, Equality, and Fraternity (personifications of the French Revolution slogan and national motto of France) with black tears, suggesting the country’s detachment from the progressive principles and actions fought for in the late 18th-century revolution, when civilians toppled statues of the old monarchic order or replaced them with democratic symbols.

The subversion of historical monuments has long been at the heart of social and political mobilizations worldwide. During Black Lives Matter (BLM) protests in the United States and beyond, activists brought down or symbolically defaced commemorative statues of colonial and racist figures, including Christopher Columbus and King Leopold II. In Richmond, Virginia, a notorious monument to Confederate General Robert E. Lee was reclaimed by protesters who transformed the statue through graffiti, performance, and projections. At the height of the BLM movement, in 2020, protesters in France draped a black cloth over a statue of French military commander and colonial administrator General Joseph Gallieni.

France’s student activists have also positioned their struggle as interconnected with others. Protesters stuck a Palestinian flag atop and wrapped a yellow vest around a statue of Joan of Arc in Toulouse. Authorities promptly removed the vest and flag, sparking fierce online debate about how statues can and should be used in political protests. While some perceived the demonstration as an attack on France's national identity, others recognized the Palestinian flag as a universal bridge between distinct but related human rights struggles.

During the May 68 protests, student activists also incorporated the visual language and rallying cries of the anti-Vietnam War movement. On May 13, 1968, photojournalist Jean-Pierre Rey photographed a young French woman, Caroline de Bendern, holding the Viet Cong flag during protests in the Latin Quarter. The image, which recalls the figure of Marianne at the center of Eugène Delacroix's painting "Liberty Leading the People" (1830) earned de Bendern the nickname "Marianne of ’68," updating the French Revolution to the context of the time.

Beyond the current movement’s tactical use of public statues and monuments, explicit May 68 references have appeared on banners and protest art in recent demonstrations. Some protesters have conjured playfully riffed on Gen-Z slogans, such as "Generation 67 brings you May 68." Others use that history to spell out warnings to French authorities: "If you screw us over (or pull a fast one on us), we will give you a May 68."

item.title: The Rise and Fall of My Wikipedia Page - Hyperallergic
item.description:
Back in February, I got a Google Alert that somebody had made a Wikipedia page about me. I immediately texted my mom. She was confused — was it a good thing? Who makes these pages? She’d heard mixed things about Wikipedia.

While her suspicion over enthusiasm was initially disappointing, she had a point. I moved into detective mode and asked a techy friend I had recently met through a cyberpunk friend: “Did you make this?”

He did not. However, he was able to find the source that did, who appeared to be some man who wrote numerous Wikipedia pages mostly about female artists.

The bio he’d written for me was simple: “Laura June Kirsch is an American photographer known for her work documenting music, nightlife and alternative subcultures. In 2021, she published Romantic Lowlife Fantasies: Emerging Adults In The Age of Hope.”

While I was flattered that somebody made the page at all — what artist doesn’t appreciate getting recognition for their work? — I did find it curious how little information was included. Was I supposed to fill in the gaps? How does this work?

Three months later, I received an email from a stranger who runs a digital marketing company with a website that churns out what the kids would call “AI slop.” He wrote that my Wikipedia page had been taken down because it contained too little information and, with his help, the piece could be restored. I was immediately skeptical of him, and while the whole thing was beyond suspect, I was curious. I compiled a robust biography and included a laundry list of links to articles about my work.

item.title: Condemning Violent Protestors, Alicja Kwade to Remove Art Basel Paris Public Sculpture Early - ARTnews.com
item.description:
A monumental sculpture by artist Alicja Kwade will be removed early from public display in Paris, where it was installed part of the public program of the Art Basel Paris fair. The piece is situated on the Avenue Winston Churchill, on the doorstep of the Grand Palais, where the fair is taking place; it went on view today and will be removed on Friday, rather than Sunday, her Paris gallery, Mennour, told ARTnews in an email.

“Unfortunately, only on view today and tomorrow, as it has to be dismantled, along with other sculptures, because of the announced riots and people who simply want to resort to violence,” Kwade told her nearly 100,000 followers in an Instagram post on Wednesday. “Protest is good, but why everything has to be smashed and destroyed is beyond…” she added. “It certainly doesn’t help the cause.”

The New York Times called the Paris protests, which began as a small student movement and blossomed nationwide, “the most destructive riots in decades.” More than half a million marched throughout France on Saturday, according to the Interior Ministry. Many were peaceful but some 1,500 shops and many symbols of the state were vandalized, leading to more than 2,000 arrests. Local authorities imposed curfews.

Kwade’s 2026 piece, L’Élévation des Mondes (The Elevation of the Worlds), stands over 14 feet high and is composed of a stack of spheres in materials like rainbow sandstone, black marble, and Carrara marble. According to a description on Mennour’s website, “the sculpture explores questions of world order, power, colonization and humanity’s attempt to construct systems that explain and organize reality. At the same time, it evokes the Tower of Babel—the human desire to reach the stars and the inevitable failure of universal systems of order.” It describes the materials as “witnesses to immense natural catastrophes, tectonic processes, and millions or even billions of years of planetary history.”

Born in Poland in 1979, Kwade lives in Berlin. Besides Mennour, the artist works with New York’s 303 Gallery and Pace Gallery, Reykjavik’s i8 Gallery, and Gallery OMR in Mexico City, according to her website. Her work appears in museum collections from the Centre Pompidou in Paris to the Los Angeles County Museum of Art and the Yuz Museum in Shanghai, and she has been included in major international exhibitions including the 2017 Venice Biennale, “Viva Arte Viva,” curated by Christine Macel.

Also on view at the same site as Kwade are works by Simone Fattal, Carmen Herrera, Marcello Maloberti, Keita Miyazaki, Manfred Pernice, Niki de Saint Phalle, and Yinka Shonibare. Press representatives for Art Basel did not immediately respond to ARTnews’s inquiry about whether other works will also be removed early.

item.title: What’s Selling at Art Basel Paris? Reported Sales Top Out at $10 M. for a Richter and a Baselitz - ARTnews.com
item.description:
Top galleries are placing plenty of works for prices above $1 million at Art Basel Paris 2026. Dealer Emmanuel Di Donna told ARTnews at the Avant-Première preview on Tuesday afternoon (aka the VVIP opening) that the experience is like “drinking from a fire hose.” That was followed by the VIP preview on Wednesday.

This all came off without a hitch amid heightened security as protests roiled Paris after demonstrations by high school students against crumbling educational infrastructure and absent teachers in a local suburb literally caught fire, with thousands taking to the streets, with some resulting property damage.

The priciest work on display, on offer from Pace Di Donna Schrader Galleries, is a rare 1917 painting of a reclining nude woman by Amedeo Modigliani, Nu étendu (Lolotte), valued in excess of $100 million. As of Wednesday evening local time, there was no word on whether the piece had found a buyer, but its presence testified to dealers’ faith that top collectors would be in attendance despite the uproar in the streets.

“This opening afternoon has been very strong and collectors came ready to make decisions quickly,” said dealer Thaddaeus Ropac in an emailed statement. “Despite any worries about the demonstrations, some deciding not to travel to Paris, we already feel that it’s the most international art fair of the year.”

The fair came on the heels of Frieze and Frieze Masters, the contemporary art and 20th-century art fairs that took place in London last week. Hauser & Wirth president Marc Payot said in an emailed statement, “In the past 24 hours, we’ve sold super-rare works by Fontana, Gauguin, Modigliani and Morandi that we first introduced at Frieze. And in Paris, we are placing equally exceptional works on our stand—true masterpieces of the second half of the 20th century by Richter, Calder, Bourgeois, Twombly, Baselitz and Szapocznikow, along with new works by George Condo, Jenny Holzer, Henry Taylor, and Camille Henrot.”

Here’s every sale that has been reported as of 9 p.m. Paris time for $1 million and up.

The top prices were commanded by Hauser & Wirth, which sold Gerhard Richter’s 1965 work Rokokotisch (Rococo Table) and Georg Baselitz’s 1965 Der Hirte (The Shepherd), each for a price in the region of $10 million.

David Zwirner sold a Gerhard Richter painting for $8.5 million.

White Cube sold Julie Mehretu’s 2001 painting Rise of the New Suprematists and her 2018 painting Mumbaphilia (J.E.) for $7.9 million each.

Pace sold Jean Dubuffet’s painting La chaise (1964) for a price over $5 million.

Zwirner sold Robert Ryman paintings for $4 million and $1.3 million.

Hauser & Wirth sold a Mark Bradford for $4 million.

Zwirner sold a 1957 Joan Mitchell painting for $3.8 million.

Zwirner sold a new Marlene Dumas painting for $3 million.

Zwirner placed a Josef Albers painting for $3 million.

Hauser & Wirth found a home for George Condo’s Woman with Designer Shirt (2026) for $2.95 million.

Zwirner sold a Luc Tuymans painting for $2.4 million.

Le Minotaure sold an untitled 1922 Wassily Kandinsky watercolor for $2.2 million.

Sprüth Magers sold George Condo’s painting The Mechanical Man (2026) to a US collection for $2.2 million. The gallery sold his painting Coney Island (2026) to a European collection for the same price.

Zwirner found a new home for an On Kawara painting for $2 million.

Pace sold Lee Ufan’s From Line No. 79061 (1979) for $2 million.

White Cube sold an El Anatsui sculpture, MivEvi I (2025), for $2 million.

Thaddaeus Ropac placed Lucio Fontana’s Concetto spaziale (1953), a painting with Murano glass fragments, for $2 million.

Hauser & Wirth sold Lucio Fontana’s 1961 work Concetto spaziale (Spatial Concept) for $1.9 million.

Gladstone sold Cecily Brown’s painting This must be the place (2017–21) for $1.5 million.

Hauser & Wirth sold Philip Guston’s Untitled (1969) for $1.5 million.

Gladstone sold Victor Man’s painting Pink Chair (2012) for $1.3 million.

White Cube sold Tracey Emin’s painting You Were Part of me (2022) for $1.3 million.

Zwirner sold a sculpture by Ruth Asawa for $1.2 million.

Georges-Philippe et Nathalie Vallois sold Niki de Saint Phalle’s multimedium sculpture Cat Head Totem (2000) for a price between $800,000 and $1.2 million.

Hauser & Wirth sold Henry Taylor’s painting “WTF’s my 40 acres & my mule, you lying…” (2023–26) for $1 million.

Lisson Gallery sold Anish Kapoor’s sculpture Clear to Dark Brandy (2026) for $1 million.

Mennour sold Lee Ufan’s Response (2026) for $1 million.

item.title: Is Germany's Far-Right AfD Co-Opting Joseph Beuys? - Hyperallergic
item.description:
More than 50 galleries across Düsseldorf and Cologne have signed a letter condemning the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party's Düsseldorf faction for allegedly referencing postwar conceptual artist and political activist Joseph Beuys and poet Heinrich Heine in the promotion of an upcoming cultural policy event.

The AfD event in question, “Cultural Policy From the Right,” is scheduled to take place in Düsseldorf on Monday, October 26, and consists of a walking tour of the city's arts and cultural venues followed by a topical lecture from the party's Bundestag (parliament) member Matthias Helferich.

(Hyperallergic has contacted several signatories and was not able to independently confirm any mention of Beuys on the AfD and AfD Düsseldorf websites.)

Considered one of the more radical party members, Helferich was elected to the Bundestag in 2021 and was temporarily expelled from the AfD's North Rhine-Westphalia state branch in 2025 after leaked chats showed that he described himself as “the friendly face of the Nazis” and said he wanted to play as “democratic Freisler” (referring to Nazi judge Roland Freisler, known for his abusive courtroom conduct and imposing the death penalty on thousands, including juveniles). The politician claimed those descriptions parodied his left-wing online critics.

Helferich was also accused of dehumanizing immigrants because of an Instagram story he posted of a rear-view mirror decoration with a sentence roughly translating to “get those creatures out” and added the tag #remigration — the term for the mass deportation of migrants, listed as one of the key AfD policies on the party's website. His expulsion from the party was ultimately overturned in June 2026.

“Düsseldorf is a city whose cultural identity is characterized by openness, internationality, plurality, and the free exchange of diverse perspectives,” a section of the co-signed letter reads. “Art emerges where boundaries are questioned and where people engage in dialogue regardless of origin, religion, skin color, gender, or political stance.”

item.title: Dozens of Sculptures Dot Bondi Beach in the 2026 Sculpture by the Sea Exhibition - Colossal
item.description:
Bondi Beach, a neighborhood east of central Sydney, is about as iconic a surf spot as they come. Its eponymous crescent beach glows with golden sand, and its cliffs frame stunning scenery. In December 2025, it was also the site of a tragic terrorist attack, when two men opened fire on a Hanukkah celebration, killing 15 people. (Gun deaths, let alone mass shootings, are exceedingly rare in Australia, especially compared to the U.S.) At Bondi, heroism and a sense of community converged in its beautiful setting, reinforcing pride of place. And it’s again home, at least temporarily, to “the world’s largest free to the public sculpture exhibition.”

Sculpture by the Sea organizes an annual outdoor presentation of dozens of sculptures every year along a 1.25-mile stretch of coastline, highlighting work by artists from around the world. Styles and materials vary greatly, from geometric abstraction to myriad representational forms. Emma Anna’s “DREAM_N” resembles a giant Scrabble letter rack, while Andre Braun’s “Surface Breach” depicts a giant hand breaking free from the earth.

The show remains on view through November 2. Explore past editions and watch a video of sculptures from last year’s exhibition below. See more on Instagram.

item.title: V&A Workers to Strike at All Four Sites Over Pay, Conditions - ARTnews.com
item.description:
Unionized staff across all four branches of the Victoria & Albert Museum in London announced their intention to strike on October 29 and 30, citing stalled negotiations and allegations of “Amazon-style” working conditions at the newly opened V&A East Storehouse.

The announcement follows two planned strikes in September at three V&A museums by workers represented by Prospect Union’s heritage division and the Public and Commercial Services Union (PCS). The V&A preemptively closed the three locations in response to the strike threat, a move it described in a statement at the time as a “difficult decision.”

Staff at the V&A East Storehouse, a publicly accessible museum storage facility in East London, had voted unanimously in July to strike, claiming they are denied enough time to use the bathroom or drink water. According to a statement from Prospect, the museum has not granted the union’s “extremely reasonable request” for two paid breaks per day.

“Prospect members are dedicated to their jobs, and it is these dedicated staff who make the museum the world-class attraction it is,” said Prospect Union’s general secretary, Mike Clancy, in a press statement. Clancy also claimed that V&A Director Tristram Hunt had refused to negotiate with the unions, which he said “shows the level of disdain in which he holds his staff.”

The V&A has denied the union’s allegations about working conditions at the Storehouse. A museum spokesperson told ARTnews following the strike vote that “all our staff have access to water and toilet facilities and regular breaks while at work,” noting that neither staff nor visitors are allowed to bring food or drinks near the collection.

Among other demands, the V&A unions have called on the museum to become a Real London Living Wage-accredited employer, which would guarantee all staff an hourly wage matching London’s cost of living, currently estimated at £14.80 (about $20). The unions have also demanded a minimum 4% pay bump for workers earning above the living wage, time and a half for work on bank holidays, and measures across all V&A sites to shade outdoor spaces when temperatures are forecast at 30°C (86°F) or higher, along with better cooling in back-of-house areas.

The V&A told ARTnews that it has been negotiating in good faith with the unions since February and that its latest pay offer meets the original demands, including a 4.18 percent average pay increase, a 6.9 percent pay increase for the lowest-paid employees, also claiming to Hyperallergic that “all our staff are already paid at least the London Living Wage – and work is underway reviewing accreditation.” The spokesperson said that the museum had also agreed to 50% pay bump for bank holidays.

PCS, however, said in a public statement Tuesday that the V&A has not settled the dispute. According to the union, while the 6.9 percent pay bump for the lowest-paid staff was offered, most employees have only been offered a 3.25 percent base increase, and that the organization is “refusing to become London Living Wage accredited.” PCS claims that “several” Storehouse employees have fainted due to the ban on carrying even sealed water bottles into the storage area, and that the facilities’ water fountains are regularly out of order.

Furthermore, the statement claimed, “During private events at Storehouse, food and drink have been served in the collections hall,” adding that “Our members have even found empty beer bottles in this area the day after an event.”

“Staff deserve fair pay, safe working conditions and respect,” said PCS general secretary Fran Heathcote in the statement. “We urge the V&A to make meaningful progress and resolve this dispute.”

item.title: Melting Ron DeSantis Statue Makes a Point About Climate Change in Florida - ARTnews.com
item.description:
Among Florida Governor Ron DeSantis’s favorite activities since he took office is pooh-poohing climate change initiatives while, almost surreptitiously, working to conserve swathes of the state he represents. Now, a group of environmental activists has found a way to make him sweat.

A life-size statue of the Republican governor was unveiled in Tallahassee last week, only to begin melting in the Florida sunshine. As DeSantis’s silver-colored face slowly slipped away, a dastardly-looking skull appeared underneath. According to The Guardian, it was all part of the plan.

The installation, titled DENIAL, was made from gallium, a metal that melts at just 85.6 degrees Fahrenheit, a temperature that Florida residents are more than familiar with.

The work was organized by environmental group 350 Action, advertising agency Uncommon, and too-cleverly named production company M ss ng P eces. Its message was fairly simple: Climate change is real, whether the governor wants to acknowledge it or not.

DeSantis, whose second and final term ends in January, has been a vocal opponent of climate policies he considers excessive. In 2024, he signed legislation that removed references to climate change and greenhouse gas emissions from Florida law and limited the ability of local governments to pursue certain environmental policies.

“We’re restoring sanity in our approach to energy and rejecting the agenda of the radical green zealots,” DeSantis wrote on X at the time.

Florida, of course, has plenty of reasons to worry about rising temperatures. The state faces growing risks from sea-level rise and ferocious hurricanes. Then of course there’s soaring insurance costs, which have become a serious problem for homeowners.

The activists behind DENIAL also had an eye on November’s elections. With DeSantis leaving office, they hope the disappearing sculpture will encourage voters to consider where candidates stand on climate policy.

“The climate crisis is one of the top issues facing our planet today,” Candice Fortin, campaign manager at 350 Action, told The Guardian. She argued that candidates who reject climate action should face the consequences at the ballot box. The installation, it seems, was as much a political advertisement as a work of public art, designed to deliver its message before the whole thing melts away.

item.title: Artists John Akomfrah, Ben Rivers, and Dozens Others Defend Sally Rooney in Open Letter - ARTnews.com
item.description:
Earlier this month, the publisher Faber & Faber announced that it was pulling the books of Sally Rooney from UK shops due to the Irish novelist’s support for Palestine Action, a pro-Palestinian group designated as a terrorist organization by the UK government. Now, dozens of artists and writers have signed an open letter that appeared in the New Statesman on Wednesday in protest of the UK government’s policy.

Among the signatories are artists John Akomfrah and Ben Rivers, art historian William Dalrymple, writer and Joyland magazine editor Stephanie Wambugu, and novelist and critic Kate Zambreno. Other prominent signatories include film director Jonathan Glazer; novelists Patricia Lockwood, Ben Lerner, and Zadie Smith; philosopher Slavoj Žižek; and actors Paul Mescal and Daisy Edgar-Jones, who starred in the television adaptation of Rooney’s Normal People.

“Sally Rooney is a writer, not a terrorist,” the letter reads. “Her books must be available to the public. Their withdrawal from sale, on the basis of ill-conceived and draconian anti-terror legislation, is an affront to basic principles of free speech and expression so long taken for granted in this country. We categorically reject censorship—whether direct or indirect—and urge the government to change course, amending the legislation which has led us to this point of repressive absurdity.”

The current standoff began last year, when Rooney announced that she planned to use proceeds from her work to support Palestine Action—one month after the UK government designated it a terrorist organization, making support of the group a criminal offense under the Terrorism Act.

In a statement to the Guardian, Rooney said: “‘In July 2025, the direct-action protest group Palestine Action was proscribed as a terrorist organisation in the UK. The following month, I wrote an opinion piece expressing my intention to go on supporting Palestine Action, which is not a proscribed or otherwise prohibited group here in the Republic of Ireland.

“As a result, the fulfillment of contracts to publish my work in the UK could now constitute a serious criminal offense. After a process of consultation and deliberation, and with my full agreement, my publisher Faber has therefore determined that it can no longer supply my work within the UK. I have made every effort to be honest with the public about my beliefs and intentions, and I am wholly prepared to accept the consequences.”

Per the Guardian, Section 15 of the Terrorism Act stipulates that any person who “provides money or other property, and knows or has reasonable cause to suspect that it will or may be used for the purposes of terrorism” has committed a crime. The offense carries a maximum sentence of 14 years in prison.

After the passage of the ban, Rooney canceled a trip to the UK to pick up an award out of fear of arrest.

The novelist is one of the most celebrated writers of her generation, known for her critically acclaimed and best-selling novels Normal People, Conversations with Friends, and Intermezzo.

item.title: Ilana Savdie and Chaïm Soutine Shed the Skin - Hyperallergic
item.description:
If Chaïm Soutine hangs up carcasses to dry, Ilana Savdie dissects them with surgical precision. Pairing the Jewish Belarusian and Colombian-American artists seems obvious: Soutine wrestled the turmoil of both World Wars onto canvas, and Savdie melts modern life's cacophony into oozing creatures of our own making. Coming face to face with their work, I felt a strange mix of alienation and recognition at once.

It’s odd to stand in a New York City gallery amid these chimeras of two eras roiling with violence and uncertainty. The rebellious, frenetic hand of Soutine, who moved to Paris two years before World War I began and went into hiding during the Nazi occupation in 1940, charged his early paintings on view here with static shocks that still have the power to jolt us. In “Hanging Turkey” (circa 1925), echoing his admiration of El Greco, Soutine transforms an unremarkable scene into a portrait of torture. The plucked turkey resembles a decapitated angel, its beak open as if in anguish even after death.

item.title: “Costume Art” Is a Bad Look for The Met - Hyperallergic
item.description:
For an exhibition with such a simple title, Costume Art at the Metropolitan Museum of Art is awfully confusing. It’s also fairly problematic, but let’s start with the confusing parts. The show pairs garments and art objects to accomplish the radical task of “reveal[ing] the inherent relationship between clothing and the body,” as the website concisely explains. The artworks are meant to demonstrate the clothed body’s presence across The Met’s collection, evidently establishing the Costume Institute as the museum’s beating heart.

So clothing and the body are related, a fact to which The Met’s artworks attest. This ridiculously broad proclamation is organized into body typologies, starting with “Naked and Nude Body.” Other sections include “Anatomical Body,” “Abstract Body,” “Aging Body,” “Mortal Body,” and “Epidermal Body.” 

With around 200 garments filling the Costume Institute’s nearly 12,000-square-foot, Grand Hall-adjacent new Condé M. Nast Galleries, certain pairings do enable visitors to experience the objects “through the lens of fashion, so the art becomes embodied,” as the Costume Institute’s Curator in Charge Andrew Bolton told the Art Newspaper — diaphanous Grecian-style gowns coupled with ancient Greek vessels, for instance.

Many other correspondences come across as forced, superficial, or questionable. For example, clothing by Chet Lo, who offered fabric swatches and audio descriptions to people with blindness and vision disabilities for his Spring 2025 collection, is juxtaposed with Picasso’s painting “The Blind Man’s Meal” (1903), while a limestone votive ear with the inscription “I belong to a deaf person” (4th–3rd century BCE) accompanies a “Deaf Dysmorphia” ensemble (2023) by designer Justin Dougan-Leblanc, who is deaf. If inclusiveness is a priority, why not feature artists living with blindness and deafness — for instance, Emilie Louise Gossiaux and Christine Sun Kim? Could the constant selfies at the Lo-Picasso display be the answer? This space was once a gift shop..

Likewise, a section titled “Pregnant Body” includes several works by (cis) men, as does “Reclaimed Body.” The latter couples Michaela Stark’s body-binding outfit “Twisted” (2026) with a photograph by Hans Bellmer of one of his faceless, limbless poupée (doll) sculptures.

item.title: A New Wildlife Crossing in Colorado Has Already Cut Vehicle Collisions by 91 Percent - Colossal
item.description:
Anyone who has driven Interstate 25 between Denver and Colorado Springs knows that traffic can get… hairy. And it’s not just drivers whose safety is at risk, as animals like elk, bears, coyotes, and more also need to use the highway to access 39,000 acres of habitat. Cars and pronghorns just aren’t compatible. That’s why Colorado Department of Transportation (CDOT) set out to build a wildlife-only bridge, the largest of its kind currently in North America, which it completed in December 2025. Within the first nine months since its opening, wildlife-vehicle collisions were already down a whopping 91 percent.

Before the crossing opened, dozens of animals were killed by vehicles every year, often up to one per day during migration seasons. The overpass spans I-25’s six lanes and is completely covered in grass so that critters have uninterrupted access to habitat on both sides of the highway—and drivers face less risk and expense due to collisions. The project is one of several in progress across the U.S., including a handful more in Colorado that include underpasses and smaller bridges. Brandon Marette, a wildlife biologist with Colorado Parks and Wildlife, told CBS News, “One of the most heartwarming moments for me was when CDOT sent me a picture of an elk mama taking her calf under I-25.”

item.title: Basquiat’s Long-Unseen Riff on Leonardo da Vinci To Lead Christie’s 21st Century Evening Sale With $30 M. Estimate - ARTnews.com
item.description:
The re-emergence of a long-unseen Jean-Michel Basquiat masterpiece is a miracle the art market occasionally performs. Christie’s announced Tuesday that one will appear at its 21st Century Evening Sale this fall.

Untitled (Leonardo and His Five Grotesque Heads) will make its first public appearance in more than two decades when it leads Christie’s 21st Century Evening Sale in New York on November 19, having surfaced from a “distinguished” private European collection. The estimate is “in the region of” $30 million, according to the announcement.

Measuring 84 inches by 84 inches, the bright orange canvas responds to Leonardo da Vinci’s grotesque heads, a series of ink sketches made between the late 15th and early 16th centuries. These ghoulish caricatures were as much commentary on current events as anatomical studies, and they form a repellent contrast to the artist’s customary grace. Basquiat was drawn to A Man Tricked by Gypsies (formerly Five Grotesque Heads), c. 1493, a satirical depiction of the social unrest caused by the arrival of the Romani in Western Europe around 1420.

Basquiat carries over all five of Leonardo’s heads, along with the drawing’s irreverent edge. Where Leonardo exaggerated his subjects’ expressions with a light hand but still gave them bodies, Basquiat strips them down to their foul essence: a slimy grin, a simian grimace, and a howling mouth. Above them reads “Muy Fao,” a phonetic misspelling of the Spanish muy feo, or “very ugly.” A pink patch in the bottom-right corner contains the words “ALTER EGO,” referring to himself, Christie’s said.

“Few paintings show Basquiat so directly wrestling with the weight of art history,” Ana Maria Celis, Christie’s head of post-war and contemporary art, said in a statement. “We know Basquiat was enthralled with Leonardo’s sketches from a young age, and in Untitled (Leonardo and His Five Grotesque Heads) we see him improvising off the great Master while tackling one of the canon’s most affecting themes, The Grotesque. Characteristically, Basquiat is able to completely reinvigorate the theme, recontextualizing it among the duplicities and the excesses of 1980s New York.”

Jean-Michel Basquiat held the record for the most expensive work by an American artist ever sold at auction after Untitled, a furious 1982 skull painting, sold at Sotheby’s in 2017 to the Japanese billionaire Yusaku Maezawa for $110.5 million. (Andy Warhol reclaimed the title in 2022, when his 1964 Shot Sage Blue Marilyn sold at Christie’s in New York for $195 million, including the buyer’s premium.)

The 1982 Untitled carried a pre-sale estimate in excess of $60 million and sold for nearly double that. Untitled (Leonardo and His Five Grotesque Heads) comes up for sale at half that estimate; stay tuned to see whether demand can push its price to or beyond the artist’s record.

item.title: Düsseldorf Galleries Sign Open Letter Against Far-Right Political Party’s Attempts to ‘Co-Opt’ Joseph Beuys - ARTnews.com
item.description:
More than 30 galleries based in Düsseldorf, Germany, signed an open letter last week that called out the far-right Alternativ für Deutschland (AfD) party for its attempts to “instrumentalize Düsseldorf’s art and cultural history to serve a political narrative that promotes social exclusion.”

Published on October 15 and initiated by Daniela Horn, the founder of Van Horn gallery, the letter centers around an event that was initially set to be staged at the city’s Heinrich Heine Institute on October 26. That event, titled “Culture Policy from the Right!,” will no longer happen at its intended venue, however, because of what Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung called “organizational reasons,” citing a Düsseldorf city official.

The letter says that, on the AfD’s website, the party mentions the poet Heinrich Heine and the artist Joseph Beuys, two figures central to Düsseldorf’s history. “We, the galleries of Düsseldorf, firmly oppose this attempt to co-opt the history and cultural heritage of our city for a partisan political agenda,” the letter reads, referring to the AfD’s attempts to dredge up new interest in Germany’s past in the hope of returning to it. “Art and culture do not belong to any political party.”

“Düsseldorf’s culture thrives on its openness—an openness that must be preserved,” the letter concludes.

It was signed by a range of Düsseldorf galleries known far beyond the city, including Galerie Konrad Fischer, Ruttkowski;68, and Sies + Höke.

The letter was also followed by a second one from Cologne galleries, with its signatories including Galerie Gisela Capitain, Drei, and Galerie Nagel Draxler. “By adding our signatures, we—as galleries based in Cologne—support this initiative out of solidarity with our colleagues in Düsseldorf. Together, across the Rhineland, we stand up for the freedom of art and culture, cultural diversity, and fundamental democratic values,” the Cologne galleries’ letter states.

item.title: Theaster Gates Returned a David Drake Jar to His Descendants—It’s Now on View at a Virginia HBCU - ARTnews.com
item.description:
In May, Theaster Gates set a precedent for restitution by transferring ownership of a stoneware vessel by David Drake, an enslaved ceramist widely known as “Dave the Potter,” to his descendants. The family estimates that some 200 of Drake’s surviving works remain in the possession of museums and collectors, though a growing number of institutions are agreeing to its request: return Drake’s work to his family, and we’ll keep it on view and accessible to the public.

The Hampton University Museum, in Virginia, offers a model of how such a deal works. The institution announced Tuesday that it will accept a loan of the vessel returned by Gates. Beginning Wednesday October 21, the work will go on view through May 2027. Drake’s piece will be in good company: the Hampton University Museum’s collection includes works by Henry O. Tanner, one of the first African American painters to earn international renown, known for his dignified depictions of Black subjects and biblical scenes; and Thomas Day, a master cabinetmaker and free man of color from North Carolina.

“It is indeed an honor to showcase this historic pottery,” Hampton University museum director Dr. Vanessa Thaxton-Ward, said in a statement, expressing “great thanks to the Drake family descendants.”

David Drake’s profile has risen dramatically within the mainstream art world over the past decade, buoyed by his biography and skill. He was born into enslavement in Edgefield District, South Carolina, bound by laws that forbade Black literacy. Defiantly, he made some 40,000 jars in bondage, inscribing many with his name and even with poems of his own devising. ARTnews named Drake’s Storage Jar, from 1857, the greatest artwork about the United States of America. (One side of the pot reads: “When you fill this Jar with pork or beef / Scot will be there; to get a peace, — / Dave.”)

In 2021, Drake set the world auction record for American pottery when his 25-gallon stoneware jar sold for $1.56 million at Crocker Farm. The following year, his art drew institutional attention with “Hear Me Now: The Black Potters of Old Edgefield, South Carolina,” which debuted at the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York before traveling to Boston, Atlanta, and Ann Arbor, Michigan. After this show, Drake’s descendants began in earnest their mission to reclaim ownership of the art.

Since 2025, the family has reportedly reached agreements of what it describes as “ethical restitution” with five museums and two collectors, including the Virginia Museum of Fine Arts; the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston; the Georgia Museum of Art, in Athens; the Telfair Museums, in Savannah, Georgia; and the Milwaukee Art Museum. Each institution contacted is offered the choice to repurchase or deaccession its jar.

“When I look at Dave’s pottery, I think about the conditions he was living in and the courage it took for him to write his name and poetry into the clay. Our ancestor left something for his family to find—a voice, a connection, a way to know him,” said Yaba Baker, David Drake’s fourth-great-grandson, in a statement, thanking Theaster Gates for his part.

Baker added, “Loaning this jar to Hampton University Museum is a full-circle moment for me. I attended Hampton, and it literally changed my life! Playing a role in my alma mater being the first HBCU to show a Drake jar fills me with joy and pride.”

item.title: The Art World Has an AI Problem - Hyperallergic
item.description:
It’s not just a problem. It’s a travesty. AI in art writing, I mean — and if those words made you instinctively cringe, then you get it, because that “It’s not X, it’s Y” sentence construction is just one of the many hallmarks of artificially generated writing. Speaking as an editor, come on. We can tell. And we will judge, and let you know exactly how we feel about it. We might even write a diatribe against it, as Senior Editor Valentina Di Liscia does today in a piece that is incisive, understanding, and original — a chatbot could never.  

An opinion piece is one way to rail against the corporate-technological surveillance complex. Bedazzling security cameras is another, perhaps less orthodox, method. That’s right: Tenured professors at MIT are gluing googly eyes and rhinestones onto the university’s cameras, Staff Writer Anna Lee reports today, to protest its investment in Big Brother. 

Sigh. To paraphrase Allen Ginsberg, I saw the best minds of my generation gluing craft materials onto surveillance apparatuses, and regurgitated as AI garbage.

—Lisa Yin Zhang, associate editor

Dear Art World, We Can Tell When You’re Using AI

Wall labels. Press releases. Artist statements. In today’s fast-paced art world, the written word stands at a crucial crossroads — and the stakes have never been higher. But here’s the thing: It’s not just about convenience. It’s about authenticity. Because the way we express ourselves matters.

The above paragraph was generated by Claude when prompted to write an introduction for an opinion piece against AI use in art writing, and if it made you recoil in your seat, you may be among those of us who have developed a strong aversion to generative text. You’ll know it when you see it: that uncanny cadence that’s overconfident in style yet hollow in substance, like a motivational LinkedIn post that feels relatable at first but leaves you with as much nourishment as a spoonful of Stevia. | Valentina Di Liscia

item.title: Can AI Help Identify the Sitters in Historical Portraits? - ARTnews.com
item.description:
Can AI help identify the sitters in historical portraits? This is the question pondered by an interdisciplinary project as well as an exhibition that opened this month at Geneva’s Musée d’art et d’histoire (MAH), showcasing a dozen 1762 chalk drawings of the family of Austria’s Empress Maria Theresa by the 18th-century artist Jean-Étienne Liotard.

Twenty years ago, when Catriona Seth was preparing to publish a book about Marie-Antoinette, she chose a beloved childhood portrait of the storied French queen by the 18th-century artist Jean-Étienne Liotard as the book’s cover illustration. Only years later, while researching the early life of this infamously decapitated royal, did she realize something wasn’t quite right. The young lady depicted in that chalk drawing has the chivalric medal of the Order of the Starry Cross pinned to her ruffled pink dress; Marie-Antoinette too received that medal but hadn’t yet in 1762 when Liotard (1702–1789) was in Vienna producing a series of portraits of the many children of Empress Maria Theresa of Austria.

As it turned out, the portrait that Seth used to illustrate the cover of her book wasn’t of Marie-Antoinette at all, as had long been believed, but rather of her sister Marie-Caroline.

“I love being able to say that to people, because it just shows that research is a continuous process and that we also learn by our mistakes,” says Seth, a French literature professor at All Souls College, University of Oxford. “There are things that can be discovered, even about great portraits, great texts. We have to think about them and question things.”

Seth had historical proof that the portrait formerly identified as Marie-Antoinette was of Marie-Caroline, but it was a trickier matter to claim the opposite: that the portrait once thought to be Marie-Caroline was actually of Marie-Antoinette. Remembering popular filters she’d seen online, Seth wondered what would happen if she uploaded the portrait into an app that ages faces by 10 or 20 years. She did so, and then compared the result to an adult portrait of the French reine. “It wasn’t very useful,” admits Seth. “But I thought: There’s an idea here.”

Seth mentioned this to Marie-Eve Celio-Scheurer, senior curator and head of the graphic arts department at Geneva’s Musée d’art et d’histoire (MAH), which holds the largest collection of Liotard portraits in the world (including the two in question). Celio-Scheurer in turn reached out to David-Olivier Jacquet-Chiffelle, a professor of forensic science and identification at the University of Lausanne, home to the world’s oldest school of forensic science. He connected with Sébastien Marcel, an expert in biometrics and face recognition.

Together, the team posed the question: Can modern AI and biometric technologies be used to identify people in centuries-old artistic portraits?

They’re attempting to answer this question through a joint experimental project, INTERART, which is a collaboration among the MAH, the University of Oxford, Idiap Research Institute, and the University of Lausanne’s School of Criminal Justice. Identifying a sitter in a portrait is a tricky art-historical task that involves a study of provenance, inscriptions, archival documentation, iconographic juxtaposition, collection history, and costume and jewelry. Could present-day technologies be another item in the researcher’s tool kit?

Results of the project, at this early stage, are part of an exhibition that opened this month at MAH titled Liotard & Marie-Antoinette: Faces Under Investigation, and an accompanying catalog. The show, on view through February 7, 2027, presents all 11 drawings of Marie-Therese’s children, plus one portrait of their father, François-Étienne de Lorraine, that recently entered the museum’s collection. In the exhibition, Liotard’s portraits of Marie-Antoinette and Marie Caroline have been newly titled to reflect the true identities of the sitters.

Current facial recognition systems, originally developed for photographs, can compare faces despite differences in pose, lighting, expression, age, and image quality. They were never intended to be used on paintings, where two portraits of the same sitter may have major differences in style and technique. The challenge, then, is to create models that can recognize facial constants regardless of changes introduced through artistic practice. One caveat: For a painting to be effectively analyzed through biometrics and AI, it needs to have been created directly before the sitter, and therefore truest to the person’s likeness (rather than a copy of an existing portrait, for example).

The potential of such a model would be to generate thresholds of probability, not provide conclusive answers. “There is never a 100 percent correct answer, and this is what also keeps the project interesting,” says Celio-Scheurer. “It gives you a potential.”

This path holds promise, but it needs refining. The algorithm can suggest associations that wouldn’t naturally occur to scholars and may help in the identification of people in portraits. “We all know museums are full of portraits of an unknown woman or an unknown man, that sort of thing, and if we can have databases of portraits where we know exactly who a sitter is, where we know exactly what their age was, we know they sat for the portrait, et cetera, then by putting an unidentified portrait into the mix, the algorithm can probably suggest things to us,” Seth explains. “It might give us leads.” In this sense, it would be a bit like a database of criminals, where you provide a suspect’s fingerprints and hope for a match.

Seth and Celio-Scheurer are careful to warn that these tools won’t replace the human eye or traditional research. Rather, they could be additional aids. “Art historians [are] quite curious about this approach. It’s not that AI will replace research in art history; it’s more of a support or tool that can give indications,” notes Celio-Scheurer. “At the moment it’s a support, but who knows how far this tool can be developed?”

item.title: Álvaro Urbano Honors the Lost Specimens of Mexico City’s Iconic Casa Cueva - Colossal
item.description:
Nested in a natural lava cave in Mexico City’s Pedregal de San Ángel region, a sprawling, mosaic-laden domicile was once home to Juan and Helen Fowler O’Gorman, an architect and artist, respectively. The pair designed the icon of modernist Mexican architecture, called Casa Cueva, in 1954, although it was largely destroyed after the couple sold the home in 1969.

At Museo Jumex, Álvaro Urbano presents an homage to the innovations of Casa Cueva, drawing on its gardens and the legacy that Helen left behind, particularly through her 1961 book titled Mexican Flowering Trees and Plants. Written and illustrated while she lived at Casa Cueva, the rich volume documented a variety of the region’s native specimens. For Urbano, these vegetal renderings became the basis of a new body of metal sculptures.

The artist’s solo exhibition, Helen, suspends his signature painted plants in a delicate arrangement. Floating against a diaphanous curtain, the lifelike sculptures appear almost as apparitions, hovering in mid-air to guide viewers through the dreamy space.

Each specimen is based off of one that appeared in Helen’s book, and a site-specific installation reveals variegated stone amid a floor of square pavers. Like Casa Cueva, the exhibition unfolds organically, creating a continual dialogue between space, plants, and those able to witness both.

Helen is on view through February 7. Explore more of Urbano’s work on Instagram

item.title: The MIT Professors Bedazzling Security Cameras to Highlight Campus Surveillance - Hyperallergic
item.description:
Tenured faculty members at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) are decorating the university's surveillance cameras with googly eyes, rhinestones, and glitzy decorations to protest its investment in what they call "Big Brother technology."

Faculty members Catherine D'Ignazio, Marah Gubar, Tanalís Padilla, Dwai Banerjee, and Karrie Karahalios began decorating the cameras in August, four months after the student newspaper, The Tech, reported that MIT would be spending over $3 million on more than 500 surveillance cameras from 2025 to 2026. According to the report, the cameras can be activated to identify faces and objects with AI, and are stationed in exterior locations and academic facilities, among other high-traffic areas around campus.

"We have these little buckets of gems and tinsel, and create these little Gumby-type creatures with googly eyes," D'Ignazio told Hyperallergic in a phone interview. None of the adornments interfere with the camera function, but are intended to remind passersby that they are under surveillance.

In a faculty newsletter announcing the deliberately unwieldy project name, "The Initiative to Beautify the AI-capable Surveillance Benevolently Installed by our Administrator Overseers and the MIT Corporation In Collaboration with Big Brother Tech Companies," the faculty members said that the campus had been transformed into an "AI-capable Panopticon."

"Many of us would not feel safer with cameras on all around us, especially not ones with AI," Gubar told Hyperallergic over the phone. While the university established a faculty advisory committee to determine whether the cameras should utilize AI technology, many eligible members were barred from participating, as first reported by local outlet Cambridge Day.

"They knew where we were coming from and what our viewpoint on the committee would be," D'Ignazio added. "Our viewpoint isn't just a matter of opinion. It's grounded in scholarly expertise. I've worked on how data, surveillance, and technology particularly affects women and marginalized groups."

An MIT spokesperson told Hyperallergic that the new cameras are "intended to close gaps in MIT’s existing security camera coverage."

Faculty took inspiration from artist and MIT alumnus Jill Magid, who rhinestoned CCTV cameras at Amsterdam's police headquarters in 2002.

"I wanted to question the visible and invisible parts of surveillance," Magid told Hyperallergic. After Amsterdam police initially turned down the artist's request to bedazzle the cameras, Magid created her own temporary fictitious company, System Azure Security Ornamentation, and successfully got herself a paid job. She advertised her business on silk screen posters that read "Big Brother in Drag," and when the larger police system shut down her enterprise, she distributed flyers urging, "Bring Back the Glam."

Faculty printed out several of Magid's posters and distributed them to students, faculty, and staff, many of whom have joined in on the seven decoration sessions so far.

While MIT Police usually only intervene by removing the decorations after the sessions, Gubar allegedly had to give her name to a suspicious officer on one occasion.

"I wasn't going to let a student or staff member give their name," said Gubar, who clarified that her tenured status protects her from severe administrative pushback.

The professor has noticed that most other participants, especially students, are hesitant to speak out about the surveillance cameras or disclose their names for fear of retaliation, an anxiety confirmed by other universities' tactics and actions. During the 2023-4 academic year, Columbia University's surveillance cameras helped administrators identify and punish pro-Palestine student protesters. In May 2026, a pro-Palestine student filed a federal lawsuit against the University of Michigan for surveilling and harassing him over his advocacy.

"The goal should be for all of us to be able to protest against surveillance, whether that be students or staff," Gubar added. "It shouldn't just be a privilege for tenured faculty."

item.title: Revisit Claes Oldenburg’s Seminal ‘Six Themes’ 50 Years After Its Debut - Colossal
item.description:
Claes Oldenburg’s (1929-2022) most famous piece of writing is his statement titled “I Am For…” which graced an exhibition catalogue in 1961 and starts:

I am for an art that is political-erotical-mystical, that does something other than sit on its ass in a museum. / I am for an art that grows up not knowing it is art at all, an art given the chance of having a starting point of zero. / I am for an art that embroils itself with the everyday crap and still comes out on top. / I am for an art that imitates the human, that is comic, if necessary, or violent, or whatever is necessary. / I am for all art that takes its form from the lines of life itself, that twists and extends and accumulates and spits and drips, and is heavy and coarse and blunt and sweet and stupid as life itself.

In all, the statement runs about 700 words. The piece is worth reading all the way through, especially for anyone stuck at a creative impasse, as Oldenburg later described it as a “slightly satirical ode or paean to the possibilities of using anything in one’s surroundings (mostly urban) as a starting point for art.” “I Am For…” is often described as a manifesto, although the artist insisted it was not. I happen to have the last line quoted above tattooed on my arm anyway.

Claes Oldenburg’s large-scale installations are iconic, typically taking everyday items and tools and ramping them up to a monumental size. Perhaps the most famous, “Spoonbridge and Cherry” (1988), was made in collaboration with his wife and fellow artist Coosje van Bruggen and has pride of place over a pond in the Minneapolis Sculpture Garden. At the entrance of the Denver Art Museum, “Big Sweep” (2006) depicts a broom whisking crumpled paper into a dust pan. And in the Sculpture Garden of the National Gallery of Art in Washington, D.C., “Typewriter Eraser, Scale X” (1998-99) depicts a giant vintage eraser with a small attached brush used to manually edit typewritten texts.

The latter motif is also one of Oldenburg’s “Six Themes,” explored in-depth from the 1970s onward. These subjects, which spurred myriad artworks apiece, consist of Geometric Mouse, Three-Way Plug, Fagends, Clothespin, Typewriter Eraser, and Standing Mitt with Ball. Sketches and material explorations prompted numerous interpretations of these seemingly mundane objects.

Oldenburg scaled up the clothespin, for example, so it stood like a giant figure, and he also produced soft prototypes made of stuffed, sewn canvas. He said that “a requirement of any subject is that it be extremely adaptable, especially in scale, so that a small clothespin would be as interesting as a clothespin a hundred feet high.”

The artist was also sensitive to objects’ potential for dynamism where we might not expect it. In “Typewriter Eraser, Scale X,” the round rubber wheel appears to careen across the lawn, its bristles getting blown back in the wind. (The first time I saw one of the Typewriter Eraser works, I thought it was meant to be a wheel that had absconded from its vehicle.)

Oldenburg privileged re-creating objects rather than utilizing found examples, so although they have a readymade-like quality, they’re anything but. He studied his source material from every angle, working with a team to fabricate giant installations that retain the familiarity of the original but challenge viewers to see them afresh. Over time, as some of the original objects have become obsolete—namely the typewriter eraser and the movie film projector, the profile view of which inspired the Geometric Mouse works—they’ve assumed an unintentional abstraction.

Several sculptures from the series go on view next month at Paula Cooper Gallery in the aptly titled Six Themes, which in turn takes its name from the landmark survey exhibition staged at the Walker Art Center in 1975. Afterward, the show traveled to the Denver Art Museum, Seattle Art Museum, New Orleans Museum of Art, and the Art Gallery of Ontario, Toronto.

The new Six Themes is an ode to Oldenburg’s seminal pieces that have not been celebrated collectively since they were first shown 50 years ago. The exhibition includes significant works representing each of the half dozen subjects, including rarely seen examples from the artist’s estate and private collections. The show opens on November 5 and continues through December 19 in New York.
