item.title: Sotheby’s London Contemporary Art Sale Tallies $61.1 M., Led by a $12.9 M. De Kooning - ARTnews.com
item.description:
In a tense saleroom with a lot of silent moments and anxious pauses—at times it felt like a courtroom, with all eyes on auctioneer Tom Eddison—Sotheby’s London conducted a slow but steady £46.1 million ($61.1 million) contemporary art sale on Thursday in a full sale room, with a £9.8 million ($12.9 million) Willem de Kooning abstraction earning the top price. The sale carried an overall estimate of £41.7–58.6 million ($55.3–77.8 million); the hammer total of £36.9 million, before the house’s fees, fell shy of the low figure.

It was a trim one-hour sale, with 34 lots, 10 of them bearing guarantees. Three works—by Damien Hirst, Anselm Kiefer, and Leon Kossoff—were withdrawn before the sale. Works by Banksy, Georg Baselitz, Jadé Fadojutimi, Lucian Freud, Gerhard Richter, and Lynette Yiadom-Boakye went unsold. Last year’s equivalent sale totaled £47.6 million ($63.3 million), led by a Francis Bacon that fetched £13 million ($17.5 million).

Sotheby’s sale on Thursday came one night after a somewhat safe but healthy evening at Christie’s that totaled £218.6 million ($289.4 million) across two sales, more than double last year’s total. The sale came during London fair week, the day after stars like Tilda Swinton and Raf Simons were seen streaming into Frieze, where many dealers reported robust sales.

“I would say the market is very cautious,” Ivana Miloradovic, art historian and consultant, told ARTnews at the Sotheby’s sale. Most of the lots, she said, “either underperformed or were at the lower end.”

The sale was led by an untitled Willem de Kooning abstract painting from 1977 that was estimated at £8–12 million ($10.6–15.9 million). Measuring 5 feet wide, it sold within estimate, hammering at £8.2 million, to sell for a total of £9.8 million ($12.9 million). The painting had last come to auction at Sotheby’s New York in 2015, when it fetched $6.1 million.

Coming in second on the night was Gerhard Richter’s 8-foot-wide Abstraktes Bild (1992), which was estimated at £6–8 million ($7.9–10.6 million); it hammered below estimate at £5.4 million, to sell for £6.7 million ($8.9 million) with fees. Thursday night’s seller picked it up at Christie’s London in 2011, paying £3.6 million ($5.7 million at the time).

The Richter was followed by an untitled dark-hued Mark Rothko abstract from 1969 that was estimated for £3–4 million ($4 million to $5.3 million) and hammered at its low estimate to fetch £3.8 million (just shy of $5 million) with fees. It last came to market in 1992 at Christie’s New York, when Thursday’s seller picked it up for $264,000.

Works by Georg Baselitz, David Hockney, Albert Oehlen, and Andy Warhol filled out the top 10, with Baselitz, Hockney, and Warhol all appearing twice.

“British sales on British soil are always joyous,” said Miloradovic, pointing to rousing demand for David Hockney’s 10th—22nd June 2021, Water Lilies in the Pond with Pots of Flowers (2021) and Butterfly Fish (1978) by Michael Andrews (1928–1995). “Everybody knows the artist, the gossip and the history. It was a homey atmosphere.”

Indeed, one of the night’s runaway successes was Andrews’s Butterfly Fish, depicting the titular animal, which hammered at £550,000 on a high estimate of £120,000 for a total with fees of £704,000 ($933,117) after an extended contest, setting a new high for a work on paper by Andrews. The artist is today less well known than his School of London peers such as Francis Bacon and Lucian Freud, but he was renowned by his contemporaries: “Mike is so economical,” fellow painter Frank Auerbach once said of Andrews. “He paints only masterpieces.”

Ottilie Windsor, head of contemporary art at Sotheby’s London, echoed Auerbach’s point in a post-sale interview. “The paintings that he did make were often bought as they were being made by a group of collectors who followed his work really closely,” she told ARTnews.” [Those collectors have] never really needed to sell and so we get very, very low supply of his work to the market; when they do come up, they really do very well.”

There were mixed results for the under-50 set, with Louis Fratino’s painting Kissing Couple (2019) bringing a within-estimate £320,000 ($424,144) and Adrian Ghenie’s The Wall (2019) likewise selling within estimate for £640,000 ($848,288). (Fratino currently has a sold-out show at David Zwirner’s London showroom.) At the same time, pieces by Fadojutimi and Yiadom-Boakye went unsold.

Getting 28 lots across the line out of 34 was still a success, Windsor argued. “Any dealer at the [Frieze] fair would be thrilled to sell nearly 30 secondary market lots.” There is both interest and money in the market, she said, “but the market continues to be selective and continues to surprise us with what it’s looking for.”

item.title: WPA Murals at Harlem Hospital Restored to Their Original Glory - Hyperallergic
item.description:
NYC Health + Hospitals’ Arts in Medicine department wrapped up conservation work on three New Deal-era murals and a John Rhoden sculpture held at its Harlem hospital on Wednesday, October 14.

Located in the hospital's indoor mural pavilion, the Great Depression-era works were made during a pivotal period in United States history when Black artists advocated for and gained unprecedented access to major public commissions through the Works Progress Administration's (WPA) Federal Art Project. Among the commissioned works were Charles Alston's two companion murals, "Magic in Medicine" (1940) and "Modern Medicine (1940)," and Hayes's eight-panel mural, "Pursuit of Happiness" (1937), which have been restored as part of the preservation effort in Harlem.

"In 1936, when these designs were submitted, administrators at the time objected to them because they said there was 'too much black subject matter,'" Larissa Trinder, head of the Arts in Medicine program, told Hyperallergic in a phone interview. After artists publicly protested the verdict, the hospital commissioner reversed the decision.

item.title: National Museum of Korea Director Scrutinized After Loaning Misattributed Work from His Private Collection to the Musuem - ARTnews.com
item.description:
The director of the National Museum of Korea, You Hong-june, has come under scrutiny after the institution pulled calligraphic artwork belonging to him from its current exhibition, according to South Korean English language newspaper Korea JoongAng Daily. Initially attributed to an independence activist, the piece was later identified as a work by a pro-Japanese collaborator.

You has exhibited and donated other items in his collection to the institution since he took office in 2025, and the incident has sparked questions about his influence on the selection of works for exhibitions.

The work at the center of the controversy was presented in the show “The Korean Table: Food, Nature, and Life” (on view through October 25) as a piece by Park Won-geun (1912–50). Park was an independence activist from North Chungcheong who fought against Japanese colonial rule (1910–1945), a dark period in Korean history marked by forced assimilation, loss of individual rights, and exploitation.

A month later, amid outside questions regarding the work’s attribution, the museum removed it from the exhibition; subsequent research confirmed that it was in fact by pro-Japanese collaborator Park Jung-yang, who had once used the name Park Won-geun.

While the museum apologized for the mix-up, it did not initially disclose the owner of the piece or how it came to be in the exhibition. You, however, admitted to lending the work, though he denied that the loan was meant to boost the value of the objects in his collection. “I did lend the piece from my private collection,” he told JoongAng Ilbo “I also believed the calligraphy was the work of an independence activist.”

The admission has spurred calls for changes to the museum’s verification process.

“A national museum should apply the strictest standards when selecting exhibits, yet it is deeply concerning that works owned or recommended by the director may bypass rigorous curatorial review,” a senior figure in the museum community who requested anonymity told JoongAng Ilbo. “Museum staff must seriously reflect on their responsibility to the public and the museum’s role as a public institution.”

item.title: Dino Bones Held in UK Museum for 100 Years Identified as New Species - ARTnews.com
item.description:
London’s Natural History Museum has millions of specimens in its collection, and until recently at least one dinosaur nobody knew it had.

A fragment of skull that spent roughly a century in the museum’s holdings has turned out to belong to an entirely new species of carnivorous dinosaur, according to Discover. Better still, the creature appears to be Europe’s first known megaraptoran, a group of formidable prehistoric predators that have prevously identified elsewhere in the world.

The dinosaur has been given the elegant name Invictibellatrix amberina, which is quite a moniker for a speciman that spent much of the past hundred years in storage.

The fossil originally came from the Isle of Wight, where it was collected by amateur fossil hunter Reginald Walter Tooley. Following his death in 1924, the Natural History Museum acquired more than 1,000 specimens from his collection, including the skull fragment. It was subsequently identified as belonging to a dinosaur, but nobody quite knew which one.

That changed when researchers decided to give the old bone a closer look. Using CT scanning technology, they examined its internal structure and produced a three-dimensional model, allowing them to study anatomical details that had previously been difficult to see.

What they found was sufficiently unusual to warrant naming a new species. The fragment, which comes from the rear of the skull, had a distinctive combination of features that researchers linked to the megaraptorans. Their findings were published in Royal Society Open Science.

Despite the name, megaraptorans were among the species of raptors made famous by Jurassic Park. They were larger predatory dinosaurs, more closely related to tyrannosaurs, although they had a rather different approach to hunting. Instead of relying principally on enormous jaws, they possessed long, powerful arms ending in a set of wicked claws.

Invictibellatrix amberina lived around 120 million years ago, during the Early Cretaceous period. Researchers estimate that it measured between 10 and 13 feet long and stood about five feet tall. It may also have sported feathers, though exactly what the animal looked like remains a matter of scientific reconstruction.

The discovery is significant for reasons beyond adding another dinosaur to the books. Megaraptorans have been found in Asia, Australia, and South America, but until now there had been no confirmed examples from Europe.

That absence presented a problem for scientists trying to understand how the animals spread around the prehistoric world. One theory holds that megaraptorans originated in Asia before moving west through Europe and eventually reaching Gondwana, the ancient southern landmass that included present-day South America, Africa, Antarctica, and Australia.

Finding one on the Isle of Wight lends weight to that theory. It also suggests that the dinosaur fauna of prehistoric Britain was more varied than scientists had realized.

Cassius Morrison, the study’s lead author and a researcher at University College London, described the long-overlooked fossil as a reminder of how much remains to be discovered in existing museum collections.

item.title: Minor Attractions, a New London Fair In a Hotel, Finds Space for Emerging Galleries and Artists - ARTnews.com
item.description:
Frieze Week in London has stopped being just about Frieze London and Frieze Masters as smaller fairs are seizing the opportunity for more intimate fair models. On Tuesday, Minor Attractions hosted its fourth edition—this time with a new location at The Newman, a newly opened hotel in central London.

This year’s fair runs until Saturday, with 38 galleries from 15 countries set up in 16 bedrooms at the hotel. Some galleries are sharing, while others have an entire suite.

“We wanted to expand our footprint and grow. We needed a little bit of a refresh,” Jacob Barnes, co-founder of Minor Attractions, told ARTnews during the VIP preview. “London’s the best city in the world and I believe that wholeheartedly because what’s happening here is more exciting than anywhere else,” he said. Despite the fair’s youth, Barnes reports that international and billionaire collectors are walking through the door. Either way, he adds, his job is engaging collectors, advisers and curators with a younger audience and “not isolating an older, maybe more established audience.”

For many of the young exhibitors, Minor Attractions is a first taste of an art fair. Kindred, a Farringdon-based record store and radio station that’s been running for six years, has become a hub for young creatives, attracting many of the city’s DJs and artists to create and network. For Minor Attractions, they will be hosting DJ sets on Friday from DVD, Temz, Angelkin, and Scar. Dancers will find in the same room artworks by Jake Walker, Felix Butterwick, Eva Delaney, and Salvi De Sena, ranging from £550 to £3,000. An abstract painting by Walker features in Kindred’s show, signalled by the artist’s former profession as a trainee dancer at the Royal Ballet School. “My work is interested in movement, notations and sound diagrams. I do some work where I start with drawings and paintings, then I use that to start choreographing, for me it’s about all these different art forms crossing each other,” said Walker.

“Galleries can sometimes feel cold and not super active in terms of what happens in that space. A lot of the artists we’re showing are people we’ve met through the shop,” said Scarlet Griffiths, co-founder of Kindred, who is also exhibiting some of her photography in the event.

“I use photography as the starting point and a lot of it goes through repetitive hand processes such as scratching or stamping, I get into a very meditative state with it,” said Griffiths, describing a piece that’s been sewn and punctured. “Photographs quite often get absorbed very quickly, but there are so many layers to them.”

Elsewhere, Goldsmiths MFA Fine Art program graduates Moses Tan and Philip Steele collaborated on an installation show consisting of luxury items scattered around the bedroom, closet and bathroom.

“I’m interested in queerness and monstrousness. I was thinking about how I’m from Singapore, where censorship is a thing and because of that, we are deemed as monstrous. So, why not put myself as a monster out there to invite people in?” Tan told ARTnews. In the bathroom, Steele placed a pair of Prada shoes and a white Prada bag with a water fountain installed in each as a statement on the life cycle of grief. “We love our handbags, but it’s about how we hide stuff and we thought about those ‘What’s in my bag?’ videos and what’s left behind in a handbag,” said Tan. Tan and Steele’s works range from £800 to £3,000, which is still more affordable than a luxury handbag from New Bond Street.

Is wellness the new luxury? That’s the question that artist duo Bora Akincitürk and Millie Rose Dobree examined in their installation comprised of remnants of palo santo, a lighter (decorated with a marijuana leaf decal), a discarded McDonald’s drink, a used condom, and tie-dye towels. In a testament to its authenticity, one of the hotel’s housekeepers trashed part of the installation. “Participating in a fair at a posh hotel gives us something to push against and a lot of the work I show and make is commenting on capitalism and consumerism with a mix of desires,” Dobree told ARTnews.

Lauren Fulcher, director at Tache, described Minor Attractions as a good introduction to the art market. Tache opened in 2025 and has since been able to present “experimental and conceptual” work without sacrificing on quality. “We have strong sales in London and Minor Attractions has been really key to that. It’s really important to have this fair exist alongside Frieze as there’s an emerging class of collectors who are international and British with purchasing power who are more interested in emerging artists,” said Fulcher. The gallery presented the work of French artist Léa Porré, who uses wood and steel in her sculptures.

Minor Attraction may be small and intimate compared to the behemoth that’s Frieze London, but the fair didn’t shy away from inviting seasoned galleries such as the London-based Cedric Bardawil and Belgium-based Tatjana Pieter, who shared a room. Bardawil has been regularly participating in the fair since its inception in 2023. He described last year’s edition, for which he showed the works of Los Angeles-based artists Francesca Gabbiani and Eddie Ruscha, “a huge success.”

“It also worked really well commercially and it was a sellout,” he told ARTnews. This season he’s showing the works of British artists Paul Housley, Anthony Banks and Hannah Tilson starting at £3,000. According to him, the work has already attracted the interest of collectors ranging in age from their mid-to-late 20s and upwards.

Pieter, who has been running her contemporary art gallery since 2005, found comfort in sharing space with Bardawil.

“It’s really important that we really start to collaborate together instead of working against each other. The art world is a little bit under pressure and we need to start working together for the bigger goal,” she told ARTnews.

Pieter exhibited the works of Brian Harte and Anneke Eussen, starting from £2,000. The decision to present artworks under £15,000 was a strategic, she said, as her collectors have been asking for “good paintings” within that range—rather than spending £300,000 or more on what is essentially an impulse buy. “We really also want to reach a new generation of buyers and keep them on. I’m often selling to young people between 20s to 40s,” said Pieter. He added, “I’m targeting collectors from the US, Europe, Asia and now China—this is why London is important, it has access to all these continents.”

item.title: Ah, the Many Smells of Frieze London - Hyperallergic
item.description:
LONDON — Yesterday, October 14, the international art world descended on Regent’s Park for the opening of this year’s edition of Frieze London, where they mingled, sipped on Ruinart champagne and spent lots of money. A visitor, coincidentally dressed to match an orange-and-black sculpture by Teresa Solar Abboud, reaffirmed that the preview day was as much about seeing art as it was about being seen.

In many ways, the 2026 edition is a typical offering. There was the obligatory mirrored artwork-slash-selfie spot, this time in the form of Anish Kapoor’s stainless-steel “Green and Brandy.” There were indeterminate objects lying on the carpeted floors, which could either be works of searing socio-political commentary or discarded wrappers from someone’s overpriced sandwich. There were lots and lots and lots of paintings. 

A novel feature of this fair — and perhaps any art fair in history — were the loo-based installations taking the form of “urinal cakes and toilet rim blocks” that are intended to “diffuse a custom scent invoking the smells of Gray Wielebinski’s studio.” Frieze commissioned the artist to conceptualize the olfactory installations for its bathrooms, which were produced by the creative studio Dean's Bottom. Maybe it was the early symptom of a fair-week cold, but I personally couldn’t detect the “notes of pencil shavings, paint, dust and sweat.” Still, though, top marks for originality.

item.title: Valerio Adami’s Hot and Cold Art - Hyperallergic
item.description:
The Italian artist Valerio Adami, who was born in Bologna in 1935, is not as well known in America as Giorgio Morandi, Alberto Burri, and Francesco Clemente, but he should be. His exhibition Alice in the Land of Violence at David Nolan Gallery, which inaugurates the gallery’s new spacious Tribeca digs, is his first in New York in more than 20 years. All but one of the 16 paintings and 15 drawings are dated between 1962 and 1967. The exception is “Hotel Pulitzer,” which the artist completed this year at age 91, and which shows no loss of acuity. 

The exhibition focuses on a body of powerful, visually innovative work done during a turbulent period when art was changing globally. In 1955, after graduating from art school in Milan and moving to Paris, Adami met Roberto Matta and Wifredo Lam. By the late ’50s, he was traveling regularly and spending time in London and New York, as well as South America and India, befriending artists, philosophers, and writers such as Richard Hamilton, Jim Dine, Oskar Kokoschka, Jacques Derrida, Édouard Glissant, and Octavio Paz. 

Even though Adami’s work of the ‘60s has been associated with Pop Art, his range of inspirations and artistic dialogues extends beyond that connection and includes surrealism (Matta’s fragmented machinery and fantastical architecture and Lam’s hybrid combinations of animal and human), expressionism (Francis Bacon and Kokoschka’s distorted bodies), and Pop Art (flat saturated colors and black outlines). Rather than being overwhelmed by these diverse styles, Adami’s syncretic approach early in his career enabled him to absorb and transform these possibilities into something all his own. In contrast to his American counterparts and their love of onomatopoeia, Adami’s paintings are full of ambiguous shapes and words that resist any reductive reading.

item.title: Rembrandt’s Ancient Obsessions Are Made Anew in Upcoming Met Exhibition - Hyperallergic
item.description:
The Metropolitan Museum of Art in Manhattan and the Musée du Louvre in Paris have joined forces to co-organize a major exhibition exploring Greco-Roman and biblical influences throughout Rembrandt's practice. As the first comprehensive presentation of Rembrandt at The Met in over 20 years, Rembrandt and the Ancients is set to open in November 2027 and will display multiple works by the Dutch master in the United States for the first time.

Assembled from both institutions' collections and a variety of international loans, the exhibition brings together over 125 objects, including Rembrandt's paintings, drawings, and prints, along with a selection of influential historic reference materials.

Rembrandt's career took shape amid a prolific period of antiquities collecting during the Dutch Golden Age, as multiple high-profile merchants and collectors, including the Reijnst brothers, Johannes Smetius, and Franciscus Junius, developed extensive holdings of Ancient Greco-Roman and Renaissance-era artifacts, texts, and archaeological objects. The relatively recent invention of the printing press also enabled the mass distribution of classical, philosophical, and scientific texts translated into Dutch.

item.title: A Landmark Survey of Native Graphic Arts Defies Expectations - ARTnews.com
item.description:
Through next February, New York’s Poster House is home to “Designed to Be Red,” a milestone survey of Native graphic arts. By institutional convention, such a show would unfold chronologically; but as its curator, the Native designer Brian Johnson, notes, time is a snake swallowing its own tail.

The show spans two centuries and more than 60 tribes and nations, organized around five themes: Indigenous Joy, Creative Sovereignty, Protest, It’s Complicated, and Extractive Marketing. The sections wrap around a single gallery, allowing visitors to begin at either end. It’s best to start from Joy, according to Johnson, though even that section’s psychedelic centerpieces—the ‘60s youthquake swept Native land, spectacularly—suggest trouble.

“Protest is literally the backbone of the entire gallery,” said Johnson, who is a citizen of the Monacan Indian Nation. Johnson assembled this show in part to correct the graphics arts record, which has both marginalized Native practitioners in its annals and left a legacy wound in the popular imagination. Americans surely remember the advertisements and have seen the movies: the heartbroken ‘Chief’, provocative princess, and proud warrior, infantilized by pidgin and hollowed of individuality.

“The whole idea behind this is multiplicity,” Johnson, who goes by he/they pronouns, said. “Native Americans and Indigenous peoples are not a single blanket. We are allowed to talk about ourselves and have ourselves seen, not as have a myth pushed onto us or woven into the American fabric.”

Among the participating artists are Kent Monkman, Onaman Collective (represented in the original posters they created for Dakota Access Pipeline protests); Anna Tsouhlarakis, who featured in the latest Whitney Biennial, contributed a banner from her Native Guide Project, that reads with the authority of Helvetica Bold: I Really Like the Way You Respect Native American Rights. The show, however, expands the notion of graphic arts beyond the boundaries drawn even by its host, Poster House. Jeffrey Gibson, who also appears in a series of jubilant collaborations with artists including Luzene Hill,Eric-Paul Riege, and Dana Claxton, is represented by a miniature ziggurat titled Because Once You Enter My House, It Becomes Our House (2020), and modeled after architecture of Cahokia, an ancient Native metropolis near modern St. Louis.

Craft, visual art, design: Where does Tony Gonyea’s ceramic wampum belt, which draws on a Haudenosaunee tradition dating to the mid-16th century, fall? And what of Ella Myers’s shadow box, Navajo Dye Chart, which, as its name suggests, displays some 40 plants and the colors they produce on wool?

“There’s a wall that is assumed, or imposed, between these categories, but someone can be a basket weaver or a rug weaver and also be engaged in graphic design. Art and design meld into everything,” Johnson said.

Read on for a conversation between Johnson and ARTnews on the show’s beginning, end, and next destination.

So, the title.

I love that the title is a double entendre: “Red” and “read.” I’m taking a racial slur and putting it right in your face, but the work is also designed to be read, understood, processed and contemplated. It’s like the Red Power movement or the American Indian Movement—taking something back that was very sacred to us and opening the entire show by punching it out.

It’s unusual to see so many three-dimensional objects in a graphic design show. What’s the thinking here?

One of the questions running through the exhibition is what counts as a poster.

For me, a poster, in a Native context, is something that communicates a message through typography, visual language or vernacular language, and is intended to be publicly shown or expressed.

Navajo Dye Chart shows how plants can be used to make different colors. The artist made posters in the 1980s, but the printing was on acidic paper and the work deteriorated quickly. There are letters still around, but I wanted the original chart—the actual object that shows where to find a particular plant and how it can be used to make a color.

That’s sovereignty: saying ‘these are the things you should be talking about.’ We don’t teach this in design history classes.

What do you make of that gap in arts and design education?

In school, we’re told that the Germans did everything, that design began with the Bauhaus, that this is how it has to be: Swiss typography. After the Bauhaus, people came to Yale, taught at Black Mountain College, and then those ideas disseminated to Cranbrook, Otis, CalArts, and other schools. Art education is stuck in the deep shadow of the Bauhaus.

[I’m a partner] at Polymode. We’ve been designing books and museum show for 20 years. In 2020, we started a school BIPOC Design History. We look at people of color who have been deliberately erased and left out of the design canon. Our school offers classes about Black design in America, Diseño Gráfico, a SWANA course—we ask designers and researchers to show us what they think has been left out.

The section “Alcatraz and Protest” further complicates the distinctions between art, object, and design.

In 1969, Native Americans occupied Alcatraz Island, off San Francisco, and held it until 1971. They issued a declaration calling for the island’s return. The settlers who had occupied the island before them had left it in disrepair. Native people realized it was no longer being used and said, in effect, “We’re taking it back.” They wrote that proclamation on a piece of stretched buffalo hide.

Where did you find it?

Emma Waggoner, a graphic designer who is a citizen of the Cherokee Nation, found it. The hide was—and remains—in the collection of the U.S. Marshals Museum in Arkansas. Waggoner and her wife drove there to scout it out. They contacted the museum, though its staff was initially unsure whether they wanted to lend it to us.

I was in Santa Fe working with an archive when the archivist said, “Hang on, I know them,” and picked up the phone. He called the museum and said, “Hey, do you have this hide thing in your collection? Yeah, there’s this Native Brian Johnson who wants to get it from us.” Again, humanity is made possible by people knowing each other.

This is a key piece because it asks why Native Americans should be held to the convention of putting [design] on paper. Why would we need a huge printing press attached to the back of a horse, moving across the plains while we’re following buffalo? We can put a message on hide and put it up. And look: there’s typography and a public message, which is why this is such an important moment in the exhibition. It’s sarcastic and truthful at exactly the same time.

From the U.S. Marshals Museum—which I just learned existed—to Manhattan. How did changing the space it’s exhibited in change the object?

Here, it’s allowed to express itself, to be present and to scream. It’s not sequestered or called a prisoner; here, it has context. Is it a sacred object? No. Is it still talking to us? Yes. It’s a protest object that helped Native people gain the rights we have today.

I appreciate that Poster House cared enough to turn off the fire alarms once the show was fully installed, allowing me to sit in the institutional space. I thanked every object, especially this one, over and over. I really lived in the preparation of the room and said, “Thank you so much for being here.”

Like many pieces here, it’s attributed to ‘Designer Once Known’. In a museum, it’s more common to see on a wall text ‘Unknown artist’. What’s the nuance?

“Designer Once Known” is what we put on the label where a museum would put “Unknown.” It’s not the same thing. “Unknown” is a shrug. It’s anthropological. No way of proving it. No way of knowing. But that’s trash. The people who made that object or that work were known. They were loved. The name didn’t fall off the object. It just wasn’t valued.

“Once Known” says somebody was real, it gives them humanity again. Somebody knew whose hands cut that block, pulled that print, beaded that pennant—their name, their Nation, who taught them, their lineage, who they made it for—all the things. So when I put “Designer Once Known” on a wall, I’m not giving up on the name. I’m filing a space with dignity and the hopes of eventually one day being able to fill that in.

‘It’s Complicated’ and ‘Extractive Marketing’ are tucked in the back, a bit out of sight. What sort of work will visitors find there?

A key piece in this section was already in Poster House’s collection: a work by Winold Reiss. A German immigrant who came to the United States in the late 1880s, Reiss became an important painter during the Harlem Renaissance. He taught Aaron Douglas painting, and his portraits of Alain Locke, Langston Hughes, and Zora Neale Hurston appeared in the Met’s Harlem Renaissance exhibition.

He was also obsessed with “cowboy and Indian” stories. Went out to the Blackfeet Reservation in Montana. Got really well known there; they loved this random German guy. He paid them to sit for him, paid for a translator, painted them exactly the way they should be painted—the opposite of Edward Curtis. Painted 280 portraits. He got to know their stories and when he died, they spread his ashes on the reservation. He also sold all those paintings to the Great Northern Railroad.

And the Great Northern Railroad—ding, ding, ding—turned those portraits into marketing tools to promote its route. The company reproduced them on playing cards, business cards. None of the money went back to the reservation. Their names were not used. They were not asked for permission.

But at the same time, the typography is amazing. That’s the contradiction. The poster is beautifully made, yet it participates in a system that extracted Native people, land, and imagery for commercial gain.

It’s complicated.

It’s complicated.

Reiss ran a workshop on the reservation?

People on vacation would come to Montana and paint Native people. They were paid, but they were also treated as a bit of a sideshow, folded into the myth of the “vanishing race.” There’s something sticky about it. Why not work with them directly, or have them teach you beadwork, something from our own traditions? No, instead, it was this Michelangelo-style, grand studio. Again, the Western idea of art education.

What’s next for the show?

This is not a comprehensive show. There’s no way we could represent all 574 [federally recognized] tribes. What about the unrecognized tribes? What about the tribes that were fully erased? Which is why I’m not the only person that can speak and do this. The show needs to go somewhere like Pine Ridge, or Oklahoma City. Wherever it goes, I’d love to dig into local archives, expanding the show to fit each space. There’s a lot of Lenape material, you know, because we’re on their land. I want the people who see it to be its anchor, so it has meaning for them.

Design is fraught in many directions, as we well know, and this show has never been done before. We have to take it to underserved areas. I need Native teenagers to see that they can make these things, that they deserve to be in this space.

item.title: Previously Unknown Canaletto Drawing Heads to Auction After Centuries in Private Hands - ARTnews.com
item.description:
A previously unknown drawing by 18th century Italian painter and printmaker Canaletto is heading to auction in England next week with an estimate of $53,000 to $79,000, after two centuries apparently spent in a single family’s collection.

The drawing, a fanciful architectural scene called a capriccio, will be on sale at Mallams auction house in Oxford on October 21. The work has been authenticated by Canaletto specialist Charles Beddington and dates to between 1746 and 1755, when the Venetian artist was working in England.

The pen and ink work shows a ruined Renaissance arcade, with vines and trees invading the crumbling stonework and a ramshackle wooden bridge that looks to be held together by wishful thinking as much as it is by rope. A boatman maneuvers his skiff out from under an archway. Broken wheels and wheels and dilapidated fences scatter the shore. Unlike the meticulously observed views of Venice and London for which Canaletto is most famous for, his capricci combined real and imaginary architecture to create scenes that never actually existed.

An inscription on the back could mean that Canaletto originally gave the drawing away as a gift. It was probably acquired in the late 18th century by Charles Burney, the English composer and music historian, and has remained with his descendants ever since.

The drawing may have been made as a preparatory study to show a prospective patron before Canaletto completed a related painting. That painting last appeared at Christie’s in London in 1995, when it sold for £380,000 (then $577,000), according to Artnet News.

Although Canaletto is most closely associated with his views of Venice’s canals and grand buildings, he began experimenting with capricci in the late 1730s. The genre gave him considerably more freedom to invent architectural settings, mixing classical ruins, waterways, and figures into elaborate imaginary landscapes.

Art historian John Rolfe told Artnet News that the works show Canaletto’s powers of observation as well as his imagination. He said the artist’s interest in the genre may have been influenced by a growing fascination with ruins, declining tourism in Venice during European wars, or his early experience working with his father, a theatrical set designer.

Canaletto’s market has produced some spectacular results recently. In July 2025, his Venice, the Return of the Bucintoro on Ascension Day sold for around $44 million at Christie’s London, setting an auction record for the artist. Another painting depicting the same Venetian ceremony fetched $30.5 million in February 2026.

His auction record for a capriccio stands at $3.3 million, achieved at Christie’s London in 1994.

The newly discovered drawing will be offered at a rather more accessible price, giving collectors a rare chance to acquire a work by one of Venice’s most celebrated painters.

item.title: Memorial Reflecting Pool Renovation Botched Beyond Previously Reported - ARTnews.com
item.description:
The long list of grievous failures related to the ill-fated Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool has grown longer after a Washington Post exposé based on an inspection report obtained by the paper.

The report, issued internally on August 6 after having been commissioned by the contractor in charge of repairs, documents far more problems than were previously known, and does not mention any vandalism of the kind that the Trump administration cited as a source of the troubles during the summer-long affair.

As reported by the Post, “The 75-page ‘failure analysis’ by Atlantic Coating Inspection includes scores of photos documenting the liner’s deficiencies—ranging in severity and including blisters, peeling and cracks—and identifies their likely causes. Some of the peeling probably occurred because workers were still applying the coating the day before the pool was refilled with water on June 4, even though the material needed 72 hours to ‘cure,’ or dry completely, according to the report.”

In a statement issued Tuesday, a U.S. Interior Department spokesperson said Atlantic Industrial Coatings (AIC), the company in charge of the repair work and that commissioned the August 6 report, “is contractually obligated to fix the Reflecting Pool” and is “well on its way to doing so.”

After AIC was awarded a no-bid $14.7-million contract to purportedly fix problems that had dogged the Reflecting Pool for decades, work commenced. As the Post recounted it, “By early June, the pool was refilled. Within days, a massive algal bloom turned the water green. Then flakes of peeled blue paint began to poke through the water’s surface.”

item.title: French Collector François Pinault Plans Permanent Hang in Venice Museum - ARTnews.com
item.description:
At age 90, collector François Pinault, founder of the Kering luxury conglomerate and the investment holding company Artémis, isn’t getting any younger. So it’s hard not to wonder how that may have factored into his latest announcement in a rare interview with Le Monde, stating he plans to mount a first permanent exhibition from his collection of over 10,000 artworks, opening in March, 2027 at one of his two Venice museums, the ornate Palazzo Grassi.

The display will feature 106 major artworks by 54 artists. Typically, the 2006-founded Palazzo Grassi hosts temporary shows, just like Pinault’s two other venues: the Bourse de Commerce in Paris, and the Punta della Dogana in Venice.

Pinault didn’t explicitly discuss his legacy, but when it comes to the stewardship of his collection, it remains unclear who will follow in his footsteps. He did say that the idea for a permanent hang has been brewing for some time, and has to do with concerns that his traditionally temporary shows don’t give a full-enough picture of his collection.

“Until now, the public has only been able to discover this story in fragments, as exhibitions came and went,” he explained. “A permanent display makes it possible to set works from different periods and generations side by side and to show how, beyond their singularity, certain questions endure.” With that in mind, he hopes to permanently showcase works that “have asserted themselves through their strength and their ability to withstand the passage of time.”

However, Pinault cautioned against assuming he was wrapping up his collecting, or that the permanent show served as his final word. “It is in no way a matter of freezing the collection or offering a definitive reading of it. Our view of art continues to evolve,” he said, referring to himself and his team of curators.

On that note, Pinault also offered a few insights into said view, which, over the years, has earned him a reputation for venturing toward challenging ultra-contemporary works. “My collection is eminently subjective and very often built on instinct, passion, or even anger in the face of the violence of the present,” he said, adding he was “sensitive to the way works of art can reveal the profound instability” of our times. However, he broadened this to include artworks that also “turn away from [the present] in an attempt to embody the invisible — that which precisely transcends reality,” added the man who reminds us that he often thinks of his modest beginnings as the son of a poor rural farmer.

Pinault is a rare top collector in France to gravitate toward artists of marginalized and non-Western backgrounds, who have been under-recognized in major museums, though he insists that when looking at an artwork, he pays no attention to “the passport or gender.”

“My interest has rather been motivated by encounters with extraordinary, almost shamanic figures, like David Hammons,” he said. “Bringing this African-American scene to light invites us to step off the well-trodden paths of Western art and take the road less traveled.”

item.title: Tate Scoops Up Works by Michaela Yearwood-Dan, Luis Fernando Zapata at Frieze London - ARTnews.com
item.description:
Each year at Frieze London, Tate gets to buy works on view at the fair through a dedicated fund, and this time around, the museum purchased just two pieces: an abstraction by Michaela Yearwood-Dan and a sculptural work by Luis Fernando Zapata.

Prices were not supplied by Tate, but the Yearwood-Dan painting, titled Peace Unknown (2026), was likely the more expensive work of the two. Sold by the mega-gallery Hauser & Wirth at Frieze London, the painting features bursts of yellow, blue, and green, along with text at the bottom reading: “IF THEY NOT PLAYING BY THE RULES, WHY THE F K ARE WE?” Its surface includes glitter, beads, a ribbon, and paper.

Yearwood-Dan, one of the youngest artists represented by Hauser & Wirth, has had a quick market ascent, with her auction record standing at $880,000. The London-based artist will soon have a New York solo show with Boesky Gallery and is currently the subject of an exhibition at the Whitworth Art Gallery in Manchester, England.

Zapata, by contrast, is less established. The Colombian artist had a relatively short career—he died of AIDS-related causes at age 42 in 1994—and has not had much visibility outside his home country. Yet he has gradually entered museums in the US and Europe, with the Centre Pompidou, the Museo Reina Sofía, the Guggenheim, and others acquiring his art.

Tate bought the 1992 piece Barge from a booth by Galería Elvira Moreno and Alonso Garcés Galería at Frieze Masters, a sister fair that is generally devoted to historical art. Like other works by Zapata, this one is intended to mimic the look of ancient artifacts and is made from papier-mâché.

Neither Yearwood-Dan nor Zapata was previously represented in the Tate collection.

Karin Hindsbo, the interim director of Tate, said in a statement, “The works both represent varied and complex approaches to materiality, evident in the large-scale richly layered surfaces and experimental use of natural and found materials. I look forward to the public being able to enjoy these stunning works in Tate’s galleries and beyond.”

Elsewhere at Frieze, the Contemporary Art Society gave its inaugural artist prize to Okiki Akinfe, whose work was on view at Ginny on Frederick’s booth in the Focus section for emerging galleries. Akinfe won £30,000 (just under $40,000). Ella Fleck, whose work was shown in the Focus section by Ehrlich Steinberg, won the Camden Art Centre Emerging Artist Award; she will now have a show at the titular art museum.

The Contemporary Art Society also spent £100,000 ($132,500) at the fair, acquiring three works: one by Claudia Alarcón and Silät from Proyectos Ultravioleta’s booth; one by Karimah Ashadu, the winner of the Silver Lion at the 2024 Venice Biennale, at Sadie Coles HQ’s booth; and one by Gala Porras-Kim at Sprüth Magers’s booth. All of these works will enter the collection of the Whitworth.

Through its own dedicated Frieze fund, the Arts Council England spent £90,000 ($119,300) to buy works by Armando D. Cosmos, Oliver Osborne, Hannah Quinlan and Rosie Hastings, and Laurie Smith. These works were respectively sold by Phillida Reid, Union Pacific, Arcadia Missa, and Wschód.

item.title: The Wildlife Photographer of the Year 2026 Winners Showcase Nature’s Power and Vulnerability - Colossal
item.description:
Federico Veronesi received the top honor of the 2026 Wildlife Photographer of the Year for his poignant black-and-white image of a female elephant carrying her deceased calf. The portrait represents a rare insight into animals’ habits we have yet to fully understand and demonstrates the power of timing and persistence in photography.

Veronesi had been tracking elephants in the Huab River Valley of Namibia when he encountered some unusual drag marks on the earth. He eventually caught up with the family, and the adult emerged with the calf’s leg wedged between her trunk and tusk. “Behaviours centering on death have been observed in both Asian and African elephants, including vocalisations, guarding the dead, inspecting and handling bones, and carrying the deceased,” a statement says. “Some researchers suggest these behaviours could indicate an elephant’s journey to understanding death, while others interpret these actions as possible displays of grief.”

Additional winners include Kutub Uddin’s capture of elegant slime molds, Loren Elliott’s portfolio featuring the coyotes of San Francisco, and Amelie Davis’ portrait of a bee coming in for a landing on a flower in Surrey, England, in the 10 and Under category. “This year’s winning photographs demonstrate the extraordinary power of wildlife photography to help us see nature differently,” says Dr. Doug Gurr, Director of the Natural History Museum. “Together they remind us that every species plays a role in the complex web of life, and why understanding and protecting the natural world has never been more important.”

At 65,403 entries from photographers in 121 countries, this year’s competition saw the largest turnout of submissions in its 62-year history. Categories run the gamut of photojournalism, wetlands, plants and fungi, behavior, portfolios, youth categories, and more. The 100 top images from this year’s contest go on view tomorrow, October 16, at the Natural History Museum in London, where they’ll be exhibited through July 11, 2027.

item.title: Jazmine Hayes Charts Community Displacement, Resilience in Brownsville Art Commission - Hyperallergic
item.description:
Last month, three New York City agencies unveiled a new $128 million multi-service center in Brooklyn's Brownsville neighborhood, featuring an extensive public art commission by local artist and community educator Jazmine Hayes.

Through the Department of Cultural Affairs' (DCLA) Percent for Art program, Hayes's four-part commission, I Am Protected (2026), graces each entryway to the building with symbolically empowering designs that channel the cultural history of Brownsville's residents and carve out space for youth ambition and curiosity.

“I genuinely want any child that walks through this door to be and feel protected,” Hayes said in an interview with Hyperallergic. “I want them to have affirmations of care, support, and community.”

Born and raised in the adjacent neighborhood of East New York, Hayes knew Brownsville well and was excited at the opportunity when DCLA reached out, especially after completing another public artwork nearby for the New York City Housing Authority's (NYCHA) Brownsville Houses the year before.

item.title: Seeing Like John Berger - Hyperallergic
item.description:
The writer and critic John Berger — that “anarchist-angel,” as essayist Megan O’Grady calls him in a review of his new biography — very much shaped the way we see. Berger himself had asked the novelist Tom Overton to wait until his death to write his biography; arriving nearly a decade after, the result is perceptive, illuminating, and an aesthetic work in its own right. 

It’s good reading when paired with Channelle Chevelle Russell’s review of an exhibition of Deana Lawson’s photographs at Gagosian Gallery in Manhattan. Lawson turns her camera’s gaze to beauty-supply surveillance photos of customers, which are often pinned behind the counter to deter theft. The gallery does not allow visitors to take photographs of the exhibition. 

The resulting questions are deeply Bergerian, if I may: Who gets to look? Who gets looked at? Who has the power to determine what an image means?

—Lisa Yin Zhang, associate editor

John Berger in His Own Bruised Time

These days, we tend to take his ideas for granted: that art — making it or contemplating it — creates knowledge. That by foregrounding the processes by which we see, we can discover the mechanisms and deceptions through which we make meaning. And, of course, that it’s important to know who is footing the bill. John Berger, who died in 2017, was famous not for challenging the Western canon but for making its revelations feel so evidently connected to everything else about life. His essays often read like personal letters, offering to us the gift of our own passions and imaginations. | Megan O’Grady
