item.title: “Cornell 7” Case Sparks Fury and Protests in Solidarity With Jane Doe - Hyperallergic
item.description:
Washington, DC — Approximately 250 protesters gathered beside the Washington Monument on the National Mall on October 8 as part of a National Day of Action event calling for accountability and justice for sexual assault survivors. The protest was just one of more than a dozen “I Am Jane Doe” demonstrations held across the country last week, “from the frat house to the White House,” as described by the Women’s March.

The National Day of Action was largely organized in response to allegations that seven Cornell University men, now known as the “Cornell 7,” gang raped a female student and advertised it in a fraternity Snapchat group. When the woman, known as Jane Doe, reported the incident two years ago, two of the men she accused were expelled, while the rest were required to write essays. Two years after the university’s response, Jane Doe’s lawyer filed another suit. 

“We are in a moment of reckoning,” Dani Bensky, a vocal Jeffrey Epstein survivor and victims’ advocate, thundered into the microphone. She was one of six speakers who called for the passage of legislation to hold abusers accountable, including Alva Johnson, a 2016 campaign staffer who publicly accused Trump of sexual assault, and Claire Barnett, a JD candidate and president of Advocates Against Sexual Violence at Georgetown Law. 

Protestors cheered them on and lifted signs reading “History Has Its Eyes on Us” and “Give Me Back My Girlhood, I Had It First.” 

Among them was activist and curator Nadine Seiler, known for her work on the preservation of artworks in the Black Lives Matter memorial fence. She held a poster that with the words “I Am Jane Doe” spray-painted on one side and “rapists are not victims” on the other, a response to criticism from the Cornell 7 and their supporters that these men’s lives were disrupted when their photos and names were shared online as part of calls for justice. Seiler told Hyperallergic that she was deeply offended by these arguments. 

“I am a victim of sexual assault, and so are many people. Our experiences are important and life-changing,” Seiler said, adding that the argument that “boys will be boys is old.” 

Days earlier, on October 5, hundreds of Cornell students staged a campus rally against the Ivy League school’s administration, expressing solidarity with Jane Doe and calling out what many view as a toxic and openly sexist fraternity culture.

When asked about the choice of location for the action, protest organizer Riley Reed told Hyperallergic that they wanted to situate survivors and advocates against the backdrop of recognizable DC emblems, with the Washington Monument obelisk behind them and the White House in sight.

“It’s a big statement [that] we will not accept sexual abusers in the White House, and we have one currently in the White House,” Reed said, referring to the multiple sexual assault allegations against President Trump.

“We want to hold the leaders at the top accountable for their actions, and this is a pretty poetic and powerful spot between the Monument and the White House, which are symbols of power,” Reed continued.

The protest lasted two hours with speeches, chants, and eventually music performed by two singers with guitars that called on Americans, in Johnson’s words, to “vote the rape regime out of office.”

As the group marched towards the White House and dispersed, Johnson’s words still hung in the air: “I am not afraid. They feed off fear, so we starve them with courage.”

item.title: Sara Flores Paints What the World Stands to Lose - Hyperallergic
item.description:
A long canoe floats onscreen to the throbbing hum of insects; a frail woman expertly strips bark from a tree. She boils it slowly, a small tamarin monkey curled on her head like a crown. Dipping a blade into a bowl of tree juice, the woman free-hands a series of geometric shapes. Her nails are stained with age and ink, her grip remarkably steady.

Directed by Èlia Gasull Balada and Matteo Norzi, The Hummingbird Paints Fragrant Songs (2026) follows artist Sara Flores throughout her rapid ascendance to art world fame as the representing artist of the Peruvian pavilion at the current Venice Biennale. The film will screen at the 50th annual São Paulo International Film Festival starting on October 19, and will make its United States premiere as the opening night selection at DOC NYC on Wednesday, November 11, streaming online as part of the festival from November 12–29.

After an opening sequence set deep in the Amazon rainforest, we encounter Flores smiling at a flute of champagne on a first-class flight to New York. At her exhibition at the now-defunct Clearing gallery on the Bowery, she stands proud in a crimson blouse, admiring the admirers. In Central Park, she feeds the pigeons after watching a man extend acorns to the squirrels.

item.title: Peter Nagy, Adventurous Artist Turned Sharp-Sighted Dealer, Dies at 67 - ARTnews.com
item.description:
Peter Nagy, an artist who became a star of the East Village in 1980s New York before ascending as one of India’s leading art dealers in the 1990s, has died at 67. Nature Morte, the New Delhi–based gallery that he ran, said that he had battled a long illness in a statement posted to social media.

“He lived exactly as he chose: fearlessly, irreverently and wildly free,” the gallery wrote. “He had no patience for convention for its own sake, and endless patience for ideas, for artists and for the people he loved. He made the art world more daring, more generous and far more interesting.”

The arc of Nagy’s career was an unusual one. He fostered a generation of appropriation-minded artists based in New York and helped stake a claim for India’s importance to the international art world. And in his art, he found his own take on commodification and reproducibility, two notions frequently addressed by artists of his generation.

In his own practice, Nagy pondered heady subject matter related to the corporatization of art and transmission of ideas and images across the globe. His works of the 1980s borrowed corporate logos and pictures from art history textbooks, showing that everything and anything could be endlessly copied until it signified nothing much at all. These early pieces synced with the bitter mindset of the Pictures Generation of the late 1970s and early ’80s, whose artists took up appropriation as a means of testing authorship and ownership.

“People don’t have anything to express, except the trademark,” Nagy said in one interview from the early ’80s. “We’re being fed information all the time.”

Relying on his education in design, Nagy would often clip out images and collage them together, using a similar method enlisted to create paste-ups used in the creation of print media in the pre-Photoshop age. He excised elements of floor plans, art books, and advertisements, then mashed together. Often, he would then Xerox the collages, blowing them up in the process.

The works looked machine-made, even when they were not. “The irony is that they’re handmade paintings that look like they might be computer-derived,” he told ARTnews in 2020 amid a revival of interest in his art. “I was interested in the degradation of the image and the information the image contained. I also thought there was additional information to be gleaned from that degradation. I was really into this idea: making copies of copies and noticing how long the original information maintained its integrity the longer I continued.”

Nagy went on to exhibit his spare art during the mid-’80s with International with Monument Gallery, a New York space that brought early attention to Jeff Koons, Ashley Bickerton, and Peter Halley. Later, he showed with dealers Jay Gorney and Nicole Klagsbrun.

At the same time, Nagy was running Nature Morte, which he founded with Alan Belcher in the East Village in 1982. He initially ran the gallery out of an East 10th Street storefront that he and Belcher rented for $500 a month. “We had no fucking clue what we were doing, but it was small and it was easy,” Nagy said the 2020 ARTnews interview. And yet, the space would go on to make a substantive mark on 1980s New York.

Steven Parrino, an artist whose punkish paintings defiled the aesthetic purity of the modernist monochrome, had his first solo exhibition with Nature Morte in 1983, the same that Gretchen Bender, a video artist known for stealing televisual material from the airwaves, also made her debut there. Cady Noland, Louise Lawler, Sherrie Levine, Robert Gober, Richard Pettibone, and others of note also showed at Nature Morte early on before its closure in New York in 1988.

Nagy continued working as an artist in the years afterward, eventually shedding his austere black-and-white collage aesthetic to make colorful paintings and installations in the ’90s. And then, for a while, he stopped doing solo exhibitions altogether. There was a 23-year interval between his 1997 Nicole Klagsbrun show and his next New York solo show, which got considerably more notice: a 2020 Jeffrey Deitch exhibition staged in collaboration with Magenta Plains, which now represents Nagy.

At the same time, Nagy was putting down roots in India. In 1992, he relocated to New Delhi; he spent the next five years moving between that city and New York. In 1997, he formally opened Nature Morte in New Delhi.

As Nagy recalled, being an artist with any stake in the market was confusing for many observers. “I am conscious of being penalized for being a dealer: Artists aren’t supposed to be interested in the market (ha ha), and my choice is, apparently, seen by some as opportunistic and manipulative,” he wrote in Artforum in 1999. He also added, “I prefer the combination of market, media, creativity, and personality that comes together in a gallery.”

Peter Nagy was born in 1959 in Bridgeport, Connecticut. He attended New York’s Parsons School of Design, studying communication design, art history, and theory; he graduated in 1981. During his time at Parsons, he began making works that he described as “large-scale, black-and-white drawings influenced by Futurism.”

He quickly ascended in the New York scene, exhibiting in the 1985 Whitney Biennial via the collective Group Material, whose installations often combined objects produced by others. That same group brought Nagy’s art to the 1987 edition of Documenta in Kassel, Germany.

Today, Nagy is best known as a dealer, with Nature Morte continuing to maintain operations in New Delhi and Mumbai. Its roster today includes giants of Indian art such as Vibha Galhotra, Subodh Gupta, Jitish Kallat, Bharti Kher, Mrinalini Mukherjee, Pushpamala N, and the Raqs Media Collective. Dayanita Singh and Vivan Sundaram also previously showed with Nature Morte. The gallery, a mainstay at fairs ranging from the Armory Show to Frieze, has previously made attempts to broaden its reach, formerly operating branches in Berlin and Calcutta.

Nagy viewed Nature Morte’s Indian iteration as a project born from the impulse toward globalism in the art world. But he also cautioned that such globalism had its downside.

Western curators, he said in a 2010 Art in America interview, “often approach Indian contemporary art with very little knowledge of India itself, so they tend to misinterpret or even ignore artists that may have great relevance to the Indian context but seemingly little to the international context. But, hey, cultural translation is one of the obvious pitfalls of the globalization of the contemporary art world.”

More recently, interest in Nagy’s art of the 1980s has grown, thanks in part to the 2020 Jeffrey Deitch show. “How amazing to discover that Nagy’s early output, which shows the artist’s penchant for mapping transformations wrought by expanded media, increased corporate power, and concentrated flows of capital, felt downright prescient today,” wrote critic Jan Avgikos in his Artforum review of that show. “Like Warhol, Nagy was practically clairvoyant in his observations about art and its commodification, the ballooning culture of the copy, and our ongoing anxieties about authenticity.”

item.title: Getty Images Files for Chapter 11 Bankruptcy Following Failed Merger with Shutterstock - ARTnews.com
item.description:
Getty Images, a massive image licensing company with hundreds of millions of assets in its library, is filing for Chapter 11 bankruptcy. According to The Hollywood Reporter, the company plans to undergo a restructuring process and emerge as a private company, with support from billionaire Charles Koch’s investment firm, by the end of the year. (ARTnews and THR are both owned by Penske Media Corporation, which has had an exclusive global media partnership with Getty Images since the fall of 2022.)

The bankruptcy announcement on Monday follows a failed $3.7 billion merger between Getty Images and Shutterstock, a rival photo and video licensing marketplace, announced in January 2025. The goal at the time was to “combine in a merger of equals transaction, creating a premier visual content company.” The new company would be called Getty Images Holdings, Inc.; Getty Images’s chief executive Craig Peters would stay on as CEO of the new entity.

Instead, a year and half later, the deal was off, due to a regulatory roadblock in the UK that would force Getty Images Holdings, Inc., to sell off the editorial side of Shutterstock, which the board of Getty Images viewed as a nonstarter. At its earnings call in August, THR reported, Peters said that Getty Images had spent more than $100 million on the failed Shutterstock merger.

In the coming months, Getty Images plans to transition from a publicly traded company to a private one, with the help of some $500 million from Koch Equity Development, which has backed Getty since 2018. A Getty Images spokesperson told THR that the bankruptcy process would not involve layoffs, nor would the company’s operations, content partners, or vendors be impacted.

item.title: Roy Lichtenstein Has Lost His Luster - Hyperallergic
item.description:
Roy Lichtenstein’s paintings stick in your mind. They are memorable and congenial. When I went to Roy Lichtenstein: Like New, the first major survey of his work in more than 30 years, at the Whitney Museum, I expected to be surprised by something new the curators dug up in their research into the sources of many of the more than 130 paintings, sculptures, drawings, and prints on view. I was not initially disappointed. 

Throughout his life, Lichtenstein credited Hoyt Sherman, his teacher at Ohio State University, with teaching him how to see. Lichtenstein gave his first son the middle name “Hoyt” and, after becoming successful, endowed the Hoyt L. Sherman Studio Art Center at the university in the 1990s. Sherman developed an experimental program where students were shown objects briefly in a darkened room and asked to draw them, an experience that is the opposite of traditional life drawing classes. Near the beginning of the exhibition, there is a darkened room with a 15-minute video reenacting one of Sherman’s “Flash Labs.” Artist Alex Da Corte, also one of the curators of the show, acts as Sherman; he wears prosthetics, and playfully teaches the class. Hung on the wall, at different heights, are some of Lichtenstein’s works from the ‘60s. 

Da Corte and his team also recreated four murals, including “Greene Street Mural” (1983), which is nearly 100 feet (~30.5 m) in length, and “Super Sunset Billboard” (1967) in the museum’s west-facing window, so museum visitors can time their visit and see two sunsets at once. I think these and other jokes muddied the waters of a famous artist widely celebrated for his charming, emotionally empty (or should I say repressed?) paintings drawn from comic strips, advertising, and paintings by other famous artists, including Pablo Picasso, Claude Monet, and Chinese classical masters such as Mi Youren. Perhaps they didn’t want us to think too long about what happens when charm loses its allure.

item.title: Utah Groups Sue Trump Administration Over Nine Mile Canyon Construction Project - Hyperallergic
item.description:
Months after the Bureau of Land Management (BLM) approved a road expansion proposal to expedite oil tanker truck transit through Utah's Nine Mile Canyon, three environmentalist groups have joined forces on a lawsuit to stop the project from progressing. The filing parties claim that the Duchesne County proposal will inevitably damage various Indigenous petroglyphs, historic structures, and the habitats of threatened wildlife species.

The Southern Utah Wilderness Alliance (SUWA), the Nine Mile Canyon Coalition (NMCC), and the Center for Biological Diversity (CBD) jointly filed the complaint on October 6, alleging that the Trump administration deliberately obscured and sidestepped the approval process and rejected the public's requested involvement in the decision.

The three organizations accused the BLM of failing to analyze and disclose the potential impacts of revising the existing roadway and the projected traffic increase on a cultural, environmental, and historic level. The complaint notes that the federal agency did not consult the United States Fish and Wildlife Service regarding foreseeable impacts on endangered and threatened wildlife species — including the Mexican spotted owl — and was in violation of multiple preservation and land use acts through its procedural omissions.

The BLM declined to comment on the matter, citing pending litigation.

item.title: Karachi Biennale Cancels Fifth Edition Over “War Conditions” - Hyperallergic
item.description:
The Karachi Biennale in Pakistan announced the cancellation of its fifth edition in an Instagram statement on Friday, October 9, citing logistical constraints and uncertainties amid "war conditions prevailing in the region."

Originally scheduled for January 16 through January 31, the biennale was to welcome artists to Karachi, the largest city in Pakistan and the capital of its Sindh province. It is not yet clear what specific circumstances or events in the region contributed to the cancellation, which reportedly occurred without the input of the biennale’s curator, Noor Ahmed, according to the Pakistani newspaper Dawn’s cultural imprint, Images.

"Artists and partners have been contacting me and they are all quite disappointed about how communications and commitments with them are being handled," Ahmed told Hyperallergic. For the past 13 months, she engaged over 100 artists and practices for the biennale and enlisted three individuals to co-curate sections of the event.  

The Karachi Biennale Trust, which organizes the event, has not replied to Hyperallergic's immediate request for comment.

item.title: ‘Arcana Borealis’ Summons the Power of Spirituality and Artist Communities - Colossal
item.description:
Around 1906, Hilma af Klint was living in Stockholm, where she kept a studio. Deeply engaged with Christian esotericism, she channeled her mystic visions into a series of otherworldly paintings that art historians acknowledge to be the first known abstract works in the canon, a paradigm shift in 20th-century art that had previously been credited to Wassily Kandinsky starting around 1910.

What continues to awe us today about af Klint’s works is she didn’t view her vibrant paintings strictly as artworks, but as a result of spiritual channeling. Their production also coincided with a period of incredible scientific discovery. Nikola Tesla had just developed the alternating current (AC) electricity system, plus generated the first radio transmissions, when he then used to create a remote control. And 1905 was Einstein’s “miracle year” with the publication of his seminal theory of relativity.

A major exhibition titled Arcana Borealis—Northern Women and Esotericism deep-dives into the history of modern art through the lens of women artists working at the intersection of spirituality and esotericism. Opening soon at the Ateneum Art Museum, part of the Finnish National Gallery, the show also explores the nature of artistic networks. In all, the exhibition gathers more than 200 works by 50 artists to broaden perspectives on women’s creative practices guided by belief systems, ecology, and the imagination.

Arcana Borealis features notable pieces by early 20th-century artists like af Klint and Anna Cassel alongside Anna-Eva Bergman, Maja Fjaestad, Sonja Ferlov Mancoba, and contemporary artist Outi Pieski. Visitors will encounter paintings, sculpture, textiles, stained glass, video, and much more that curators Dr. Nina Kokkinen and Dr. Marja Lahelma conceive as a challenge to “art historical narratives that have privileged the myth of the lone artistic genius,” the museum says. Instead, Arcana Borealis highlights how collaboration and spiritual communities shape the artists’ practices.

Cassel and af Klint worked together, for example, as part of what became known as The Five, a group of Stockholm-based women who explored spiritual realms through séances and meditation. Collaboration also comes to the fore in Pieski’s performance titled “Guhte gullá / Here to Hear.”

Pieski collaborated with dancers and choreographers Biret and Gáddjá Haarla Pieski, drawing on their Sámi heritage and incorporating vibrant clothing in a nod to traditional garments. The Sámi are an Indigenous people in predominantly the northern regions of Norway, Sweden, and Finland, and performance speaks to the trauma inflicted by state-sponsored assimilation programs and discrimination going back centuries.

The exhibition takes its title from the Latin arcana, meaning “hidden knowledge,” and borealis, meaning “the north.” The show “approaches ‘the North’ as a cross-border cultural and imaginative space shaped by mythology and spiritual traditions,” the museum says. “It traces how artists across Finland, Sweden, Denmark, Norway, Iceland, and Sápmi turned to esotericism, alternative cosmologies, meditation and mediumistic practices to explore questions of existence, creativity, and belonging.”

Arcana Borealis opens on October 23 and continues through February 28, 2027, in Helsinki. You might also enjoy navigating into the arcane through Taschen’s Tarot, part of the publisher’s Library of Esoterica series.

item.title: Meet the Lap Easel, a Portable Companion for Taking Creativity Anywhere - Colossal
item.description:
From birch plywood and select solid maple, birch, cherry, and other native hardwoods, Chicago maker and designer Bill Groot crafts handmade Lap Easels in small batches. It’s perfect for a multitude of creative activities, like drawing and painting, reading books and magazines, writing, relaxing with a screen, holding a cookbook, and more.

item.title: Phillips to Sell Rare Amedeo Modigliani Sculpture for $35 M. During New York Sales - ARTnews.com
item.description:
With the hope of catching Modigliani momentum evident at auctions in Europe over the past couple years, Phillips is bringing a rare sculpture by the Italian-born modernist to the marquee New York sales in November with a hefty price tag.

Modigliani’s Tête (1911–12) will hit the block with a $28 million–$35 million estimate. If it sells, the sculpture will be one of the most expensive three-dimensional works ever sold at auction by the artist, who is best known as a painter of female nudes with almond-shaped eyes.

The sculpture belongs to a larger series of heads, examples of which are generally held by major institutions, from the Metropolitan Museum of Art to the Tate museum network. This one was carved from a block of limestone and features a slender face with a long nose and a tiny, smiling mouth.

Modigliani is thought to have produced around 28 sculptures during his short lifetime. Twenty-six of them survive.

Calling Tête a “masterpiece,” Phillips deputy chairman of the Americas and senior international specialist Jeremiah Evarts said in a statement, “Fresh to the market after over half a century in the same important private collection, Tête embodies everything that makes Modigliani’s sculpture so revered, including its profound art historical importance.” (The house did not identify who had previously owned the work, which last changed hands in 1972.)

Tête is not likely to become the most expensive Modligiani sculpture ever sold, however. In 2010, Christie’s sold another stone head for $52.8 million, in what was then Modigliani’s overall record. The same auction house sold another Tête in 2019 for $34.3 million.

Modigliani’s current record, it is worth noting, is far higher than the upper end of Phillips’s estimate for its Tête. That benchmark stands at $170.4 million, as minted by the 2015 sale of his 1918 painting Nu couché, which remains one of the most expensive artworks ever brought to auction.

Still, Phillips is likely hoping to catch a wave of market interest in Modigliani evident in auctions staged over the past two years. In 2025, at Christie’s in Paris, a portrait by the artist sold for $31.3 million, tripling its estimate and setting a new record for the artist in France. Then, earlier this year, a painting of a nude woman from the collection of Joe Lewis sold for $63.5 million at Sotheby’s in London, creating a new record for Modigliani in Europe.

item.title: Vermeer the Immortal - Hyperallergic
item.description:
Vermeer is everywhere. Not only in the hallowed halls of museums, but also in the gentle light that streams through the window just so, or in the crisp pages of a love letter set down gently at one’s writing desk. Historian Ruth Bernard Yeazell seems to agree in Vermeer’s Afterlives, her new title tracing the Dutch painter’s enduring presence across the arts, from film to verse. Lauren Moya Ford brings us into its exquisitely illustrated pages.

In another must-read today, a glitch at Finnegan Shannon’s Pioneer Works exhibition yields insights on institutions and accessibility. “The installation’s deviation from what I expected, like disability itself, offered me a new perspective on the world,” Bryan Martin writes, “a reminder of our collective responsibility to those who live in it.”Hyperallergic Halloween is around the corner. RSVP for our art costume party with snacks and an open bar in Brooklyn on Wednesday, October 28 — members get discounted tickets!

—Valentina Di Liscia, senior editor

Finding Vermeer in Unexpected Places

As strange as it may sound, Johannes Vermeer’s fame is a relatively recent phenomenon. The Dutch painter known for his exquisite, enigmatic interior scenes fell into obscurity shortly after he died deeply in debt at only 43 years old in 1675. Vermeer was barely a footnote in the annals of art history until the mid-19th century, when the Parisian critic Théophile Thoré rediscovered his work. “Here’s someone we don’t know in France, and who very much deserves to be known!” the writer proclaimed in 1866. | Lauren Moya Ford

item.title: Who Are the Most Faked Artists in History? - ARTnews.com
item.description:
What makes an artwork real? This seemingly straightforward question can actually be quite loaded.

A faked artwork is generally considered to be a copy of an existing work. This seems clear enough, but what about when an artist copies his or her own work? A forgery, on the other hand, imitates an artist’s style to create a new work. But what if the forged artist was someone who challenged concepts of artistic originality and appropriated images from others?

Art trickery can get tricky. And yet it persists. Some experts estimate that around half of the secondary art market consists of forgeries and misattributions. Certain inauthentic works—made by infamous forgers such as Han van Meegeren (who made bogus Vermeers) and Wolfgang Beltracchi (responsible for hundreds of phony works)—are prized for their novelty and tales of exposure. Other times, artworks can initially be written off as forgeries but later identified as genuine through scientific analysis.

Museums are not impervious to these phenomena. The Metropolitan Museum of Art, for example, has a 1624 portrait of Spain’s King Philip IV that it deemed in the 1970s to have been created by an assistant to Diego Velázquez, only to reauthenticate it fully to the Spanish Baroque painter in 2010.

When in doubt, experts lean on the three-legged stool of art authentication: stylistic scrutiny, provenance, and scientific analysis. (The Velázquez reattribution was thanks to the latter, after varnish removal.)

In a comprehensive 1963 book titled Forgeries, Fakes, and Reproductions, author George Savage writes at the close of the preface that “the collector may take heart from the fact that at no time during the history of the art-market has forgery been so difficult as it is now, or more likely to be detected, and the forger’s task is becoming continually more difficult.” Be that as it may, it doesn’t appear that forgers have stopped in the decades since.

Below are nine of the most faked and forged artists.

item.title: Can Daniel Weiss Fix the Philadelphia Museum of Art? - ARTnews.com
item.description:
Daniel Weiss had a part-time job as a stock clerk in the gift shop at the Kennedy Center in Washington, D.C., while in school at George Washington University studying psychology and art history. When his boss was fired for substantial revenue losses, Weiss told the people in charge at the Kennedy Center: “I think I can fix this.” He was offered a six-month tryout the week he graduated in 1979, and over the next four years continued to run the retail business and supervise a staff of 175.

It wouldn’t be the last time he stepped in to fix things.

“Along the way, I realized I was interested in pursuing graduate training in art history, but I also had an interest in how organizations function,” Weiss said this summer at the Philadelphia Museum of Art, where he started as director and CEO last December, a month after the board of trustees fired his predecessor, Sasha Suda. While at the Kennedy Center and throughout “the rest of my career,” he explained, “it became clear to me that if one cares about culture and the arts and higher education, one has an obligation to care also about how these institutions are run.”

Weiss, now 69, is widely viewed as a smart and thoughtful straight shooter, skilled at solving organizational problems. With an MBA from Yale and a PhD in Western medieval and Byzantine art from Johns Hopkins, he had a long career in academia, working in tandem as president and professor at Lafayette and then Haverford colleges, before being hired as president and chief operating officer of the Metropolitan Museum of Art in 2015. In his eight years at the Met, he helped steer the institution out of a $40 million financial deficit and through a change in directors and internal culture. Now at the PMA, which is also facing a major budget deficit after years of high staff turnover and low morale, Weiss is being looked to as a steady hand to right the ship.

“Dan brings a combination of qualities that’s uncommon,” said PMA board chair Ellen Caplan. “He obviously understands art and scholarship, but also how to lead large, complex organizations. He has a proven track record and a compelling vision for the role that museums play in society right now.”

When Weiss stepped down from the Met in 2023, his plan was to teach, write books, spend time on his boat, and, he said, “just live the life of somebody who wakes up not in charge of anything.” He took a faculty position at Johns Hopkins, where he had begun his teaching career in 1993, and was asked by several institutions, including the PMA—on Suda’s introduction—to advise on governance practices. “I’m something of a voice in that area,” said Weiss, who articulated his views on the importance of shared governance at mission-driven institutions in his 2022 book Why the Museum Matters.

Working with the PMA’s board on a governance review over the next two years, Weiss “got to watch, from a fairly close point of view, the dissolution of Sasha’s relationship with the institution and the board,” he said. After Suda’s termination in November 2025, according to the public record, she filed a lawsuit contending that she was fired “without a valid basis,” and pushed to have a jury trial; the board responded that “Suda misappropriated funds from the museum and lied to cover up her theft.” A court ruled early this year that the matter would be settled privately in arbitration, as per a clause in Suda’s contract.

The board’s decision to terminate Suda was made “completely independent of anyone that we were going to bring in to follow up,” Caplan said. “One had nothing to do with the other.”

Weiss said that at first, when the board approached him to step in, he was hesitant to take the helm. “My initial reaction was: ‘I’m not your guy,’” he recalled. “On the other hand, I thought, I know how to do this. I understand the issues. Maybe we can get this place back on track, where it’s doing what it should in the world.”

According to a veteran of the New York museum world, speaking on background, Weiss’s replacement of Suda could have at least the appearance of opportunism. “Dan, who is a consultant to the board, slip[ped] into that job really quickly. He has a way of being like a board whisperer,” said the person, adding, “I’m not saying that there weren’t reasons for both Dan to accept it and the board to do what they were doing. Things are never that black and white.”

Asked if the PMA board had considered conducting a search for a new director, vice chair Osagie Imasogie said the trustees had unanimously agreed to appoint Weiss to the position. “If you look at the market for top-notch leaders in museums of the caliber of the PMA, it’s just a handful of people who would fit that profile,” he said. “There was no point in going through a performative process when we already had the best person we could think about.”

If the board had brought Weiss in on only an interim basis, that would have diminished “the full authority to get on with the work that needs to be done,” Imasogie added. “It was also important that we ensure stability be brought back to the institution after the challenges we have had.”

In his work with the governance committee, Weiss had presented to the full board. “There was an immediate comfort level, both because we knew Dan,” said Jennifer Rice, chair of the governance committee at the time, and “he also came with such a stellar reputation for the work he did at the Met.”

DURING AN INTERVIEW OVER LUNCH in his office, Weiss came across as direct and efficient, at once businesslike, candid, and personable. Before addressing the first question he was posed, he paused to point out that, like his interviewer, he, too, wore a coin on a chain, pulling from underneath his shirt and tie a third-century Hellenistic coin with the image of Alexander the Great, given to him by his family. “I’ve worn it around my neck for 25 years,” he said. “It feels like a connection to the ancient world and the continuity of human existence.”

Born in Newark, New Jersey, and raised on New York’s Long Island, Weiss described himself as “a completely lackluster student” early on. Wandering into an art history survey class at GW, he fell under the spell of a charismatic young professor who was a medievalist. “He changed my life,” said Weiss, who is friends with him to this day. “That was where it began for me.” With his dual graduate training in art history and business, Weiss began teaching at Johns Hopkins as well as writing books; by the time he was tenured, he’d also become involved in administrative work. “I knew how to run a meeting and had experience in things that most faculty don’t,” he said. He rose to the position of dean in 2001, before moving in 2005 to lead Lafayette College for eight years, then Haverford College for two. He described being very surprised when the Met approached him.

“I’d never worked in a museum before, and they were asking me if I wanted to run it,” Weiss said. “They were looking for someone who could bring management and fiscal knowledge and experience into a role that was also completely sympathetic and sensitive to the mission. It opened up a world for me that I didn’t really plan on.”

In his first weeks on the job, he dug into the museum’s financial statements and discovered that what had been presented to him as a modest $4 million deficit on a budget of more than $300 million was, in fact, a $40 million deficit.

“The museum was drawing down reserves in ways that weren’t really kosher to meet operating deficits,” he said. “We had been overspending and, as it were, undermanaging the institution, and it had resulted in various patterns of accommodation to these problems that were not fully transparent to the board.”

Under Tom Campbell, a former tapestries curator promoted in 2009 to director and CEO after the retirement of Philippe de Montebello, who had led the Met for more than 30 years, the museum had been investing heavily in its digital operations as well as its modern and contemporary satellite, Met Breuer (which operated in the former Whitney building from 2016 to 2020).

“To Tom Campbell’s credit, I made him aware right away of a very substantial deficit, and he was perfectly willing … to do whatever it took to figure it out,” Weiss said.

Campbell would ultimately resign under pressure in 2017. The Met’s board voted unanimously that Weiss would assume the title of president and CEO, and that a new director would report to him. Max Hollein was appointed to that role in 2018, and by 2020, working together, the two leaders had balanced the budget. When Weiss stepped down in 2023, Hollein assumed the additional title of CEO.

“Dan is a leader who doesn’t shy away from complex issues,” said Candace Beinecke, cochair of the Met’s board. “His tenure at the Met was defined by his tremendous commitment to the museum’s mission. Working in partnership with the museum’s director, he steadily and effectively helped lead the Met through crucial moments. He brings deep analytical skills, expertise, and a strong sense of purpose to his work.”

Central to Weiss’s management at the Met was his reinforcement of the principles of shared governance. “It starts with the relationship between the CEO and the board,” he said, “but all the constituencies that have a vested interest in the well-being of the institution—the curators, the professional staff, the mayor’s office, the unions—also need to have a voice.”

Weiss enlisted the staff as partners in helping to fix the deficit, creating a task force of some 15 representatives to advise on budgetary decisions. They were part of tough conversations about how to cut the program, cut salaries, make layoffs. Weiss’s proposed changes to the museum’s longtime admissions policy of “pay what you wish”—after a decline of 67 percent in the average fee people paid during the previous decade—was controversial internally. The task force gave presentations to every department to involve the staff of 2,000 in the logic of Weiss’s proposition.

“We went through a long, difficult process to find the right approach based on principles, economic interest, and what’s best for the institution,” Weiss said. The new policy, instituted in 2018, maintained “pay what you wish” for New York State residents, who already support the Met through their taxes, but charged $25 (since raised to $30) for out-of-town adults. “In the end, it generated the revenue we needed, and it had no negative effect on visitation,” he said. “It was one step of 40 that we had to do to bring the budget into balance.”

A longtime Met employee, speaking on background, described Weiss as popular overall with the staff. “He was accessible, somebody you could talk to,” the employee said. “He’s a very rational, reasonable, and reasoned man.”

Weiss also instituted a review process at the Met, requiring the board to evaluate his own performance annually and perform a “360”—including feedback from employees—every other year. He later required the same for all department heads at the Met. “You must be accountable to the people you lead,” he said, noting that nobody would ever have given de Montebello a review. “I think it was a great disservice to Tom Campbell, who was a brand-new leader with no experience, not to have a performance evaluation of any kind.”

What Met trustee and former board chair Daniel Brodsky appreciated most in working with Weiss was “his willingness to listen,” he said. “He made time for staff at every level of the museum, and he genuinely cared about creating an environment where they could do their best work. During a period that included leadership transitions and the pandemic, that steady approach served the museum well.”

The PMA—RANKING IN THE TOP FIVE largest encyclopedic art museums in the US by both physical and collection size—now stands to gain from Weiss’s brand of leadership.

In late July, The Philadelphia Inquirer reported that the museum had a deficit of $10 million on an operating budget of $76.5 million and that its leadership expected the deficit could grow to as much as $15.9 million in the next year. Weiss said his goals for his first year are to fully assess the museum’s finances, rebuild the senior leadership team, and move forward on an action plan with open lines of communication across the board and staff.

In 2020, during the tenure of Timothy Rub, who led the PMA from 2009 to 2022, more than 400 staff members signed a petition calling for accountability changes in the wake of complaints about the behavior of former managers. Later that year, the staff voted to unionize. Museum workers went out on strike in 2022, on Suda’s first day on the job as new director (she chose to cross the picket line).

“Over the last several years, staff levels have decreased very dramatically,” Weiss said, from some 500 employees five years ago to about 385 now, through a combination of attrition, firings, and layoffs to reduce operating costs. “At the same time, the programmatic ambition during Sasha’s years here was very high, so there was more to do and fewer staff to do it. That led to a really strong sense of disappointment and frustration.”

Weiss has recently recruited Mitchell Wein, from the Brookings Institution, as executive vice president, chief financial officer, and chief operating officer; Lavita McMath Turner, from the Met, as chief people officer; and Neil Batiancila, from the Philadelphia Zoo, as chief advancement officer. He’s also promoted longtime curator Jennifer Thompson to deputy director of collections and exhibitions, to work alongside Jessica Smith, chief curator.

“I didn’t want a hiring freeze when I arrived, because the institution couldn’t survive that way—you have to have people in the right jobs,” Weiss said, acknowledging that he had added to the expense base. “We’ll balance the budget—it’s just a matter of exactly how. I know what the levers are.”

Caplan said that Weiss’s consistent internal communication on his action plan—addressing nine areas, including facilities, visitor experience, technology, and security—has already helped with morale. “He’s continuing to provide updates on progress being made or challenges he’s facing, and that transparency is appreciated by both the staff and the trustees,” she said.

Weiss appointed an internal task force to reevaluate a controversial rebranding campaign rolled out last fall under Suda, which included the institution’s name change to the Philadelphia Art Museum (mocked by critics as “the PhArt Museum”). A collaborative decision was made early this year to reinstate the original name but keep the new logo, featuring a griffin—a decorative architectural element repeated across the museum’s 1928 Beaux-Arts building.

The plan for a second phase of an ambitious expansion—originally approved by the board in 2004, during the tenure of Rub’s predecessor, Anne d’Harnoncourt, then designed by the late Frank Gehry—is now on hold. (The first phase of the plan was completed under Rub in 2021, for $233 million.) “We have a series of deferred building maintenance issues that have to be addressed before we return to the question of the Gehry project,” Weiss said.

He believes the museum’s current annual attendance of about 675,000 is “way too low,” he said, given the size and quality of the institution’s world-renowned collection of more than 240,000 objects and its stature in the city. But he has yet to set a specific target number for visitation, or dig into the question of admissions cost. “We feel very strongly that admissions pricing is a necessary evil, but whatever we do has to work for Philadelphia, so people come,” he said. The museum’s endowment—now almost $600 million—could always be better, Weiss said, but “it’s totally respectable.”

Weiss, who has committed to staying through 2028, told The Philadelphia Inquirer that he expects to have the budget balanced in three years. He and the board will then decide whether he will continue on for longer, he said, stating firmly, “I’m not going to stay 10 years.” He and his wife, a corporate healthcare lawyer whom he met at GW, live near the museum in a high-rise building. In Easton, Maryland, where he serves on the board of the Academy Art Museum, among several other institutions, they have a second home, with an extensive book collection that reflects Weiss’s diverse interests. His boat remains docked in the marina there.

While the skills of museum leadership may be transferable, Weiss recognizes that he is “not operating on the same patient,” he said. “The PMA is not the Met. They have different issues, different cultures, different communities. You need to listen very carefully and take what you know and apply it respectfully to this place in this ecosystem. I don’t have it all figured out.”

item.title: The Trafficker Who Furnished the Museums of LA - Hyperallergic
item.description:
In a 1940 photograph by Man Ray, Academy Award-winning actor Teresa Wright poses misty-eyed alongside an ancient Chacmool sculpture. The reclining figure, with its head contorted toward viewers, offered a refreshed vision of modernity to both Hollywood stars and a growing clientele of collectors and museums interested in pre-colonial art from ancient Mesoamerica. In 1947, for instance, the Minneapolis Institute of Art purchased a “King Chak Mool” for $10,000. That sculpture toured Europe as part of an exhibition from 1958 to 1960 and quickly became a cornerstone of the museum’s collection. Just a decade later, one specialist made a dreaded discovery: The sculpture was a forgery.

This story, and that of the gallerist at its center, is chronicled in Artifacts to Art: Collecting Ancient America in Midcentury L.A. (2026) by Andrew D. Turner, Mary E. Miller, and Khristaan D. Villela. The book elaborates on the various conditions that shifted the classification of “pre-Hispanic” artifacts from anthropological items of study to art objects that could be collected by museums and patrons alike. It also helped answer a question I’ve always had about Los Angeles museums as a curator myself: Why is so much cultural heritage of ancient Central and South America preserved in our city’s collections?

As Artifacts to Art discusses, the Stendahl Art Galleries were a key driver in the illegal looting, smuggling, and sale of these objects to its Los Angeles clientele. The Galleries’ archive is now housed at the Getty Research Institute (which published this book), allowing for a deep investigation into the shady dealings of an art dealer who had little regard for the cultural histories he exploited. Turner, Miller, and Villela present five years of groundbreaking research into that archive here. Over its non-chronological chapters, the book describes the various forces that collided to create a market for these objects, including revered international museums, Hollywood actors, and looters across Mexico.

item.title: A Little Fantasy Goes a Long Way - Hyperallergic
item.description:
“Abandon the search for Truth; settle for a good fantasy.” These words, taken from Fran Lebowitz and written on the wall to warn all ye who enter Luhring Augustine’s Chelsea gallery, set up the premise for its current group show: settle for a good fantasy.

It’s an admittedly juicy quotation. So juicy, indeed, that the gallery has hung Shaun Pierson’s photograph of a very voluptuous strawberry — seriously, it’s like the Venus of Willendorf of strawberries — right next to it, as if to underscore the point: Photography is always chasing a fantasy.

The exhibition’s main room leans into this, showing portraiture's fragmentary, erotic side. Works by Pierson, David Seider, and Janice Guy vacillate between intimacy and unknowability, like a fractured peep show. Curved, freckled backs touch. Beautiful shards of women’s faces are pieced together, seemingly pulled from the dark. Guy’s grids of self-portraits from the 1970s are particularly arresting, and not just because she also happens to be beautiful.

item.title: NYC to Provide Free Art Supplies to Grantees - Hyperallergic
item.description:
Materials for the Arts (MFTA) is launching a new free shopping program for artists who receive city-funded grants on October 19, nearly three weeks after Mayor Zohran Mamdani and the Department for Cultural Affairs (DCLA) announced that they are doubling grants for individual artists and small nonprofits in New York City. 

The new MFTA program functions as a free supply base for the selected artists, who can now receive up to $10,000 in city-funded grants, which had remained at a $5,000 cap for the last 20 years. The organization will open its 35,000-square-foot warehouse to artist grantees on the second Monday of every month (apart from federal holidays) from 3 pm to 6 pm, offering materials such as leather spools originally used to make airplane seats, tomes dedicated to the visual arts, and dinosaur masks. The first iteration of the program will take place on Monday, October 19.

“By broadening our operations to offer shopping days directly targeting these art grantees, we can ensure that more artists, more changemakers, and more New Yorkers have access to our city program,” Tara Sansone, the executive director of MFTA, told Hyperallergic.

item.title: Finding Vermeer in Unexpected Places - Hyperallergic
item.description:
As strange as it may sound, Johannes Vermeer’s fame is a relatively recent phenomenon. The Dutch painter known for his exquisite, enigmatic interior scenes fell into obscurity shortly after he died deeply in debt at only 43 years old in 1675. Vermeer was barely a footnote in the annals of art history until the mid-19th century, when the Parisian critic Théophile Thoré rediscovered his work. “Here’s someone we don’t know in France, and who very much deserves to be known!” the writer proclaimed in 1866. 

Thoré was drawn to Vermeer for the same reason he still fascinates museumgoers today: His small selection of attributed paintings — some 35 to date — and still-hazy biography spark more questions than answers. But in the three and a half centuries since his death, Vermeer’s mysterious works have also inspired a wealth of visual art, cinema, poetry, and literature.

These artistic echoes are the focus of scholar Ruth Bernard Yeazell’s Vermeer’s Afterlives (2026), a richly illustrated exploration of the artist’s enduring and remarkably widespread impact through a careful survey of works made in his mythologized shadow. From Danish painter Vilhelm Hammershøi’s hushed canvases to experimental 20th-century film and sensual contemporary verse, Yeazell meticulously catalogs and analyzes the Delft painter’s iconography — especially his recurring solitary female figures gently illuminated by daylight filtered through nearby windows — and persistent commitment to open-ended interpretation over a singular narrative.

item.title: When the Accessibility Conveyor Belt Jams - Hyperallergic
item.description:
Finnegan Shannon’s There's no me without you at Pioneer Works considers the fragility of systems and the consequences of their breakdown for disabled bodies.

The installation is a 12-foot-long square conveyor belt — think conveyor-belt sushi — in a maroon-carpeted room that carries and displays objects for visitors to interact with, from plush chairs to open spaces for individuals who can’t access the seating. Masks, accessible text, hand sanitizer, DIY air purifiers, and descriptive audio are also available, defining Shannon’s vision for an equitable, gentle engagement with art.

Three artists will be presented during the show’s run. For the first month, Ariana Martinez places small objects in dishes atop the moving presentation for visitors to pick up and touch. These small, tactile, fidget-like objects range from ceramic strips to masses of rope, all of which delight. 

Unfortunately, during my visit, the conveyor belt wasn't turned on, which undermined the apparatus's accessibility intent. Staff eventually came up to switch it on, but when the machine proved stuck, they left without resolving the issue. The inert belt became a frustrating metaphor for institutions and a larger social apathy toward accessibility needs. 

Spurred by fellow visitors’ confusion, I gently rocked a jammed plate side to side to see if it would help, and the belt started moving. Although accidental, Shannon's intent crystallized. We are all interdependent. Creative solutions are inexorably linked to disability, making the subject ripe for artmaking. The installation’s deviation from what I expected, like disability itself, offered me a new perspective on the world — a reminder of our collective responsibility to those who live in it. 

There’s no me without you continues at Pioneer Works (159 Pioneer Street, Red Hook, Brooklyn) through December 20. The exhibition was organized by Pioneer Works.

item.title: Frieze’s Kristell Chadé Discusses Why the Fair Has ‘Never Been About Adding Points on a Map’ - ARTnews.com
item.description:
Editor’s Note: This story is part of Newsmakers, a new ARTnews series where we interview the movers and shakers who are making change in the art world.

In the last decade, the UK has been hit with Brexit and its aftermath, a global pandemic, and seven new prime ministers, but the country has retained its number two ranking in terms of global trade by value behind the US, according to the 2026 Art Basel and UBS Global Art Market Report. When Frieze London and Frieze Masters take over the grounds of Regent’s Park starting on Wednesday, spirits could remain high; the positive mindset may also be found at fairs like Minor Attractions and the London Invitational, which will also take place during Frieze Week.

As in the past, there remains a wrinkle: Art Basel Paris is taking place next week, and many are skipping London for that fair. However, this edition of Frieze London is bigger than the last’s years, with 176 galleries from 43 countries. In 2025, there were 160 galleries operating from 44 countries.

Kristell Chadé, Frieze’s executive director of fairs, has been with the organization for 15 years and now oversees eight fairs across the Frieze portfolio. “Global does not by any means mean uniform and we don’t export a fixed concept to the other fairs. Each fair has its own identity and as we become more global, we are more interconnected, which is a real strength for us,” she said. This year’s fair has an increased presence from South Asia; Frieze London has its first Sri Lankan participant in Saskia Fernando, for one. There’s also going to be a notable South Asian presence at Frieze Abu Dhabi next month, too.

ARTnews spoke with Chadé about London’s position in the art market, competing with Art Basel Paris, the health of the fair, and how it’s navigating Abu Dhabi amid political turmoil.

This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity and concision.

ARTnews: What is the big theme at this year’s Frieze London and Masters?

Kristell Chadé: Frieze London and Frieze Masters are our most global fairs across the board, and that’s something we’ve definitely continued year on year. The thread between the two fairs is a sense of discovery. History is being told, reexamined, expanded, and rewritten. This year, as with previous editions, there’s experimentation and ambition, putting emerging artists in conversation with established practices, and that’s always been a fundamental element of the fair. Frieze’s broader role is supporting artists through their careers, and what we did with the 2024 redesign of the fair was push initiatives around putting young voices at the forefront and make sure that all segments of the market are represented

With Frieze Masters, the focus is very different: It is rooted in scholarship and expertise. But what makes it so unique is that it doesn’t present art history as a single and linear story. The idea is really to open new connections and narratives between periods, cultures and geographies.

Frieze London prides itself on its global energy. What geographic areas are the focus this year?

We’re very pleased to see year-on-year applications from new geographies, and that’s really something we’re trying to continue to promote year after year. Frankly, for us, it’s a real indicator of success: The breadth of geographies and perspectives that you can encounter at the fair is something that we closely track and that we continue to work to expand.

The main trend this year across both fairs is an increased presence from South Asia, which is really exciting for us, especially considering our presence in the region for the last five years. Having a foot in South Asia has really allowed us to strengthen those connections. We have our very first gallery participating from Sri Lanka this year. We’re seeing a strong contingent from Brazil, which has stemmed from past curated initiatives such as the Breeze Curator Travel Grant, an initiative with the Instituto Guimarães Rosa and the Embassy of Brazil in London. The grant offers five Brazil-based curators the opportunity to participate in the fair. Another region that remains strong is South Korea, as well as the Gulf and North Africa. From the numbers we’re looking at and from the trends we’ve seen so far, we are excited to welcome more collectors from India, Pakistan, Singapore, Indonesia, Turkey, and Canada. We’re also expecting an increased number of American collectors to visit the fair this year.

It goes without saying that London is an incredible global city. We know that it remains one of the world’s most important cultural centers—it’s the second largest art market globally, and it has real appeal in that sense for galleries and collectors. London allows creative talent to thrive. We have highly regarded art schools, world-class museums, and a thriving gallery scene, probably more than most cities can claim.

London is being called the city where artists work and live taking over from Berlin. What still connects artists to this city? And what is Frieze as an organization doing to keep artists, international dealers, and collectors coming back?

We are a commercial platform, there’s no denying that and ultimately, we want galleries to be able to make sales at the fair, that’s a big part of why they participate. Our responsibility goes way beyond just the commercial aspect of the fair. Frieze London and Frieze Masters have acquisition funds that support museums purchasing works from the fair, from the Tate Fund to the new Dasha Shenkman Focus Fund.

We also have great opportunities for major commissions and exhibitions for artists who are showing at the fair such as the Frieze Artist Award and the Camden Art Centre Emerging Artist Award, those are incredible opportunities for artists and it’s a very pivotal moment in their careers. At the same time, we collaborate with a number of organizations and embassies that allow travel from different countries to the fair for curators that are based in their countries. We’ve worked with Brazil and Italy. Frieze’s mission is to turn visibility at the fair, which is something very easy to experience, into long-term support. The idea is to have a long-term legacy for the art world and the art community.

Even though people say London has lost to Paris, it’s still a city that’s dominated by all types of art fairs, from the London Invitational and Minor Attractions to Frieze. What’s your feeling about London’s art scene? Has it really lost to Paris?

The autumn season clearly revolves around two well-established centers of gravity, London and Paris. But I do think they’re different and complementary offers. Galleries and collectors choose to do both, and there’s a clear rationale for them to do so. Our best argument in favor of London is that the city has so much to offer and London remains unmatched in the richness and diversity of its ecosystem. Frieze is about discovery and London is that place for it with new artists, studios, gallery openings, and new nonprofit or artist-run spaces opening.

When it comes to business, what is the health of Frieze London and Masters right now? And are you making any adjustments?

Both Frieze London and Frieze Masters galleries are full with really strong and diverse galleries, that speaks for itself. For the actual numbers, we do have slightly higher numbers of galleries and countries this year, which is always an interesting data point. However, beyond just the numbers, what’s helpful for us is to look more specifically at the quality of the content and breadth of what’s being represented at the fair.

To your question around adjustments, we’re not a fixed model and we’re conscious of our responsibilities—we talk to galleries all the time, also collectors, advisers, museums and those conversations really inform our decisions. We know it’s a demanding time for galleries who are under a lot of pressure. We know costs have gone up across the board and that galleries, especially mid-sized and younger ones, have to make decisions and are thinking very carefully about where they show, why, and what. And I think that’s actually healthy. We don’t want to have a fixed model when the world around us is evolving so quickly. We represent all segments of the market, from international blue-chip to established mid-market galleries to younger, more emerging galleries. They’re all equally important constituents for us to consider.

What are the challenges that Frieze as an organization is facing right now?

The pressure that galleries are under and how it forces us to think on our feet probably is the biggest challenge that we’re facing right now. Over the last few years, we have shown how we’ve been able to make changes and respond to those shifting requirements. If you think about gallery pricing, we always aim to keep annual increases minimal, if not keep the prices flat year-on-year where possible because we are conscious of the financial impact on our participating galleries. In 2024, we introduced a sliding-scale pricing model to help galleries make the move from Focus into the main section of the fair—it’s something that’s very dear to our heart in terms of supporting that next generation of galleries. We also have a number of curated sections that have lower entry points and what we’re trying to do is have different ways for galleries to participate, depending on where they are in their careers and what their priorities are at certain point in time, which artists they’re working with, and what part of their program they’re keen to show at the fair.

The fair’s first curated thread is devoted to a hot topic—queer visual history. How did you decide on “Queering Modernism” during such a shaky political climate?

It shows that Frieze acts as a platform for what is happening in the world and gives opportunities to encounter themes and ideas that are sometimes radical and sometimes new to provoke reactions and discourse. For us to be part of that discourse and conversation is ultimately what we thrive to do. The section is an example of how closely we work with curators and we find our legitimacy in our collaborators. We shine a spotlight on curators, artists, and galleries.

Frieze started in 2003 and has grown to include eight art fairs. How has this growth been possible? How are you partnering up with other countries, but still having a point of difference?

When I started at Frieze, we only had one fair. The growth over a decade has never been about adding points on a map. We wanted to see what Frieze could bring to each city’s existing ecosystem or a gap in the market. London is all about that trailblazing energy, whereas New York is a snapshot of what’s being made today: It’s the epicenter of the global art market. In LA, there’s a strong civic engagement that runs through everything we do from gallery presentations to artist projects. Seoul is the balance between tradition and cutting-edge practices, and Chicago is rooted in the midwestern community. When Abu Dhabi happens next month, it really takes its roots in the growing ambition of the cultural offer that the Emirate has been building. For us, global does not by any means mean uniform, and we don’t export a fixed concept.

You’ve been at Frieze for almost 15 years. How has your role changed, but also the business of running an art fair?

I came to the role from the gallery perspective. I was initially working very closely with all the galleries that participated in the fair, and that’s been quite instrumental for the growth of the business and how we’ve strategically expanded. We feel very strongly that what we do is for galleries—they remain our core constituents. A part of my role is to try and make sure that the Frieze voice is maintained and carried through all that we do.

As Frieze Abu Dhabi gets ready for its opening in November, it’s been an unsettling time for the Middle East. How are you navigating that?

We’re approaching the situation with open communication with all our galleries and collectors, both in the region and around the world, because it is another international fair. There’s a strong appetite for the upcoming fair and it’s an important milestone for us and the region. We’re cognizant of the context, and we’re in close contact with our local partners to ensure that everything runs very smoothly. Frieze Abu Dhabi follows the same logic as every other fair that we’ve started. It is a combination of a very specific cultural moment for that city as well as an opportunity for galleries. Abu Dhabi as a city offers an existing infrastructure and credibility—it has built a very ambitious ecosystem on Saadiyat Island, where the fair will take place, and it includes world class museums such as Louvre Abu Dhabi, the Zayed National Museum, the Natural History Museum Abu Dhabi, and the Guggenheim Abu Dhabi opening in December.

The fair has existed for 17 years, but with our takeover, we’re bringing the Frieze expertise and scaling it internationally by building on solid foundations in the region, which already has an engaged community. Abu Dhabi is rapidly growing with artists, galleries and collectors—the ingredients are all there.

Have any galleries dropped out of the fair because of what’s happening politically?

We have had transparent conversations with everyone involved. With every fair, there’s a level of flexibility with the gallery list. We have a full fair; everyone who’s participating is bringing very high-quality work, and part of that is shaped by the fact that we’re always working with talented curators and partners. We will have our usual Focus section for younger galleries and Frieze Masters Abu Dhabi is curated by Marika Sardar with the idea of exploring the history of cultural exchanges across the Indian Ocean. Global Futures, curated by Tarini Malik, will focus on cultural histories from the region.

It’s been 10 years since Brexit was announced. How has this affected Frieze London and Masters?

The facts speak for themselves. The UK remains the second-largest art market globally, after the US, where we’re also heavily present. By nature, we operate across different continents and cities, meaning that we have to constantly adjust to the changing landscapes of different regions. London is where it all started, and there’s such a good understanding of the opportunities that are possible here. We’ve been able to capitalize on the rich ecosystem that supports the fair.

item.title: In Search of the Future, Artists Give New Life to Dead AI Models - ARTnews.com
item.description:
Editor’s note: This story is an edition of Link Rot, a column by Shanti Escalante-De Mattei that explores the intersections of art, technology, and the internet. The column will appear every other Monday.

The development of generative AI text-to-video models has been charted over the past few years through a simple prompt: “Will Smith eating pasta.”

The first videos, posted in 2023 using newly released Stable Diffusion models, feature a ravenous, monstrous rendering of the actor shoveling a pasta-shaped blob into his mouth with his hands, only for it to slide, morph, stretch, merge with surrounding artifacts, or simply disappear. Within three years, the test has nearly reached its endpoint, with the pasta responding naturally to gravity and interacting correctly with the other objects in the scene: the fork, the plate, and Smith’s mouth. But as each new model arrives in relentless succession, what happens to those that came before it, or to the videos produced during their training?

That question drives “Post Generation,” a new exhibition at tiat gallery in San Francisco. Three artists reflect on a video archive generated by Veo 1, a now-defunct model developed by Google in 2024. Released only for internal use, though eventually leaked, the model seemed barely functional. It could produce only six-second videos, with long waits between generations and predictably surreal results: a six-legged horse galloping across a wet field, a staticky smudge that might be children playing in a pile of leaves, and a three-limbed hominid swimming in a pool. Researchers generated hundreds of thousands of videos before the model was shut down and superseded by successive generations, Veo 2 and Veo 3, both of which were released to the public.

“Because these models are so resource intensive and because each new model is faster and more efficient, it’s hard to justify keeping old models around. No one can generate using Veo1, and the outputs it produced aren’t publicly available,” said Tina Tarighian, a senior creative technologist at Google’s Creative Lab and the show’s organizer. “So I thought, what can we do with these leftover scraps of a model? Can we gift this archive to artists?”

Tarighian shared a portion of the archive with choreographer Zelia ZZ Tan, creative engineer Karyn Nakamura, and fiber artist Haley Mortin, asking each to respond with new work. The resulting exhibition is a multimedia meditation on the nature of this technology and an archive of a particular moment in its development.

For Mortin, working with this training data was a natural extension of her practice, which incorporates AI-generated images, images sourced from research papers, and other AI artifacts into knit works. Her fascination with these artifacts stems in part from a former job as a data annotator, a form of often-invisible human labor in which workers around the world categorize and tag images to teach AI models to “see” and correctly identify objects.

“It was 2018, I had just graduated college, I didn’t know what AI was, and I needed money,” said Mortin. “I thought it was just a data entry job.”

Over the next two years, Mortin found herself solving CAPTCHA tests and labeling images not only by the objects and subjects they contained but also by more subjective categories, such as the emotion she thought a person in a photo was expressing. The Veo 1 outputs are, albeit indirectly, a product of this kind of labor. In examining them, Mortin decided to focus on the strange forms of text the model generated.

“It produced two flavors of nonsense, these glyph-like shapes or empty phrases,” said Mortin. “These [visual] models don’t learn text like an LLM [large language model] does, rather, they learn text as a texture.”

This led Mortin to consider the embroidery samplers made by women in the 18th century. Many young women first encountered writing not through ink and paper but through embroidery. As they practiced stitching text, they often used these samplers to record family histories. Mortin’s resulting work, Soup Is Made of Water (10 Samplers) (2026), comprises ten knitted pieces that capture the different forms of garbled text generated by Veo 1, reflecting on the histories of text production and the practices through which it is preserved and archived.

Rendered in black and white yarn, the pieces depict a looping scribble, a calligraphic font attempting to spell, perhaps, “beauty” [b eurt], and what can only be described as a sigil tattoo of the kind commonly inked on thighs in Ridgewood, Brooklyn. The work deftly brings into conversation, and inverts, different practices of language learning and history-making: those of 18th-century women, contemporary machines, and artists attempting to process and document a machine’s training.

Karyn Nakamura also took up Tarighian’s invitation to explore the research histories behind Veo 1 and other generative models, combining several video technologies in a single work. In Labor of Light (2016), an assemblage of technologies comes together as a kind of altar to the history of video production. Suspended from a pair of cables, a white device emits a beam of light that appears stable to the viewer but contains, in its flicker, the analog signal of Quicker ’n a Wink (1940), a film explaining how MIT’s Harold Edgerton developed the high-speed photography technology used to produce slow-motion footage.

The beam of light leads down to a projector that casts a collage of Veo 1-generated videos onto a white cloth, each clip emerging from a static-like field of vivid colors. Nakamura uses RGB noise, a key component of generative AI, in which images and videos are generated from an initial field of noise. Beneath the cloth, small toothpicks held in place with putty support printouts of landmark research papers that advanced the techniques behind modern AI generation, including diffusion.

“I find the process of image making and the process of video and video systems incredibly beautiful, there’s a lot of craft in there,” said Nakamura.

Even as someone who sees beauty in these technologies, Nakamura worries that the pace of development makes their inner workings increasingly difficult to understand, limiting people’s ability to intervene creatively and exercise agency in contemporary image-making processes. For this reason, her work often dwells in the glitches and gaps of earlier models, such as Stable Diffusion 1.5.

“Because I like Stable Diffusion 1.5, sometimes I think, ‘Oh, am I being a Luddite?’” Nakamura mused. “Like, what is even progress right now?”

Against a backdrop of increasingly morbid present and future outcomes, these artists reckon with a technology advancing at breakneck speed despite being barely a few years old. Yet in a culture that equates progress with perpetual acceleration, to pause is to risk obsolescence. Choreographer Zelia ZZ Tan explores this tension in a ten-minute dance performed at the exhibition’s opening on October 8. Combining choreography with animated avatars, the performance captures the ways bodies move and gesture in Veo 1 videos.

“I searched the archive through movement rather than only through words when I started to realize that between generated bodies, physical bodies, and the computational body, there are a lot of similarities and also a lot of rules based on how they can perform,” said Tan. But dancing with the limitation of movement of the generated body required vulnerability.

Tan continued: “It’s such an honor to have a body, to be able to be present there, and maybe I’m not showing the most trained technique, but to listen, to be hesitant on stage, to wait for something to happen – that’s part of the power of being there as a performer.”

item.title: Raven Chacon’s Echoes on Park Avenue - Hyperallergic
item.description:
It’s a beautiful Monday to celebrate Indigenous Peoples’ Day, no matter what the federal government says. In a conversation with Associate Editor Phillip Pyle, Diné musician Raven Chacon discusses his recent improvised performances at the Park Avenue Armory, the “collision” at the heart of all music, and reclaiming the technologies of colonial violence through sound.

Read on for a guide to shows centering Native art around New York City — including Shelley Niro and Sarah Sense, two of my favorite artists — and a critique of a Felix Gonzalez-Torres exhibition that bizarrely glosses over the late artist’s AIDS advocacy and political spirit.

—Lakshmi Rivera Amin, associate editor

Raven Chacon Sounds the History of the Land

item.title: Long Live Generation 6-7 - Hyperallergic
item.description:
You try to get the latest news about the inspiring student protests in France but a snarky reporter on the New York Times podcast tells you that the country’s problem is providing “too generous” pension plans and parental leaves. 

These welfare benefits saddle the country with debt, he says, scolding the government for not making France more competitive in the marketplace. 

You turn off the podcast because you can’t listen to any more of this evil idiocy. 

You finally finish reading a much-hyped new novel and wonder why you made yourself go through such torture. You return to Marcel Proust’s In Search of Lost Time to cleanse your mind’s palette. “When one is in love one has no love left for anyone.”  

You go to a gala dinner and remind yourself of the golden rule at these events: always go with the steak because you never know with chicken. You feel snazzy in your new tuxedo and remember that the last time you wore one was during the Arab Spring. 

You meet with Algerian-French artist Kader Attia in a Tunisian restaurant in Manhattan for an interview about a show he’s curating in India. His face full of wisdom and passion, he encourages you to wear your wounds on your sleeve.

In the cold morning breeze, you see two doves perching on the wing of an eagle sculpture on a tall column. You think about how all good art has some connection to music, and how houses always look good when they’re painted green. Nina Simone sings “Tomorrow will be the 22nd century” in your ears. Meanwhile, generation 6-7 is remaking May 68.

—Hakim Bishara, editor-in-chief

The Met’s Krasner and Pollock Show Is a Breathtaking Upending

I was married to an artist once. It was not a good experience, although calling it “an experience” makes it sound like a unified, parsable thing, and it wasn’t that, either. We’re all adults here, is what I’m getting at — so no one should imagine that anyone has bulletproof insight into anyone else’s romantic relationship, much less their own.

Certainly, once a relationship is over, it becomes a moving target in permanence: the good, the bad, and the ugly all trading places, each a microcosm in which various genres of chaos and ecstasy hold sway. And whatever we may think of other people’s marriages, we must take care. What we believe we know is almost always something we meant to say about ourselves. The phone call is coming from inside the building. If you see something, well, see something. | Lucy Ives
